#5002. 7 Best Shaving Creams for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Expert

Say goodbye to razor burn and hello to a better shave.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

UNLESS YOU'RE SHAVING with a top-notch wet or dry electric razor, you’ll need to first apply a product to prep the skin. There are really only two options: pre-shave oil and shaving cream. For the smoothest, most irritation-free shave, opt for both in order. However, the latter is a non-negotiable unless a red, sliced-up face is the look you’re going for. No judgment?

The truth is, your shave is only as good as the cream you use because the right shaving cream cushions the skin, reduces irritation, and locks in moisture for added comfort afterwards. It also helps the razor glide smoothly, preventing nicks and tugging.

Most importantly, it turns a tedious routine into a clean, refreshing experience. But not all shaving creams are created equal—some barely protect or soothe at all. To save your skin the abuse (and potential scars), I’ve rounded up the best options worth trying.

Jackfir The Classic checks every box I look for in a shaving cream. Its ingredients are clean, its scent soothing, and the formula protects the skin from irritation and cuts. Simply put, I got one of the closest, smoothest shaves I’ve ever had with this cream.

The creamy lather cushions the razor perfectly while aloe, cucumber, and panthenol keep the skin calm and hydrated. The scent is invigorating and woodsy, thanks to natural oils like cedarwood, vetiver, and chamomile instead of synthetic fragrances. This also makes it safe for sensitive skin without being entirely scentless.

On top of its long list of at least 70 percent organic ingredients, it even comes in sustainable packaging made from recycled materials. I generally shave with a safety razor for my face and a cartridge razor for my body (or when traveling), and Jackfir was perfect for both.

It’s slick enough that it never clogs up the blade, but thick enough to keep my skin protected. This is all on top of prepping the skin while also locking moisture in post-shave.

I have dry skin that’s prone to shaving irritation, but the combo of panthenol and bisabolol kept my face feeling calm before and after the session. You also don’t need to use much to cover your entire face; barely more than a nickel-sized amount will do the trick. The only downside to this stuff is that it’s over $35, but given how long it lasts and how great it performs, it’s well worth it.

The razor you use isn’t solely responsible for shaving irritation. For many, simply switching to a gentler, more skin-friendly shaving cream will go a long way in preventing bumps and redness. You won’t find a better option than Harry’s Shave Cream, which is no surprise coming from what I dubbed the best skincare brand for clean-shaven men.

This cream packs powerful natural ingredients like eucalyptus oil, mint oil, and aloe vera, which work together to soothe skin and reduce irritation. It’s free of parabens, sulfates, or other common irritants, and its formula is equally thick and silky to protect and smooth skin. Best of all, it could double as the best value shaving cream at only $8 a container.

I’ve been cutting my own hair for over a decade, so I really only go to barbershops for one thing: a close and luxurious shave. But this shaving cream makes me wonder if I could eliminate those trips altogether. It’s the closest you’ll get to the barbershop experience with an incredible, soft lather that feels like a hot towel wrapped around your chin. Sure, it’s a little pricey and best applied with a brush—which I count as a positive—but it’s far less expensive and time-consuming than making a trip to your local shop.

If you’re prone to razor bumps and burning like me, this cream will feel like a godsend thanks to its rich and smooth lather that’s packed with ingredients that care for skin. The aloe vera and shea butter deliver deep hydration, keeping your face calm and protected while helping to prevent razor bumps and irritation.

The pair also works together to calm inflammation, moisturize, and create a protective barrier that helps prevent razor bumps and post-shave irritation. White tea extract then adds that clean, refreshing feel I always look for in a shaving cream. It’s soothing, nourishing, and bump-free.

I don’t use cartridge razors too often, as safety and electric razors tend to leave my sensitive skin less irritated. But if I’m traveling or in a hurry, I’ll turn to them—and rarely without this shave gel from GilletteLabs. The rapid foaming is as advertised, thickening in seconds for quick application.

It gives that fresh feeling once it hits your face before the razor even touches your skin. While it’s listed as having a cedar wood and orange peel scent, I rarely catch too much of it. But I prefer that, as I’d rather rely on my cologne for fragrance.

I implore you to use a shave oil in addition to a cream to minimize irritation as much as possible; however, if you really don’t have the time or desire to, use this. Atwater’s shaving cream is designed to pull double duty, preparing the skin before the razor touches it and protecting it throughout the shave. As a pre-shave, its blend of hydrating oils helps soften stubble and create a smooth, conditioned surface.

During shaving, ingredients like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil work together to cushion the blade, reduce friction, and keep the skin nourished. This combination leaves my skin feeling as calm and moisturized as it’ll get without using a pre-shave oil. Plus, it’s completely unscented, so it’s safe for even the most sensitive skin.

Dr. Squatch’s shave butter feels more like a creamy lotion than shaving cream, allowing the razor to glide smoothly across the skin while it also moisturizes. Despite how that sounds, it never clogs up my blade—even when I use a safety razor. The trio of natural hero ingredients, shea butter, murumuru butter, and macadamia oil, is rich in vitamins and fatty acids that deeply hydrate, soften, and smooth the skin.

Together, they create a nourishing barrier that locks in moisture and helps reduce irritation for a more comfortable, soothing shave. The lotion-like texture takes a couple of shaves to get used to if you’ve traditionally used thicker shave creams or foams, but the feel of your skin during and after is immediately satisfying.

Shaving cream is often used as a catch-all term for several products that prep and protect your skin while you shave. There are three main types, and the right one depends on your razor, your skin type, and your personal preference.

If your shave is only as good as the cream you use, then the cream is only as good as its ingredients. Shaving creams often include soothing ingredients like aloe vera, which calms irritation and helps the skin stay hydrated before and after shaving. Shea butter is another popular one, as it provides rich moisture that softens hair and improves razor glide, reducing friction during the shave.

Many formulas also contain vitamin E, an antioxidant that nourishes the skin and supports repair after shaving. Then there is a slew of natural oils and other vitamins to keep an eye on, like vitamin B5, vitamin C, argan oil, and coconut oil that hydrate, soothe, and prevent post-shave irritation.

How often do you shave? That’s the most important question to ask yourself when considering the size of your cream. A larger tube offers better value and lasts longer, especially for daily shavers. Smaller sizes, on the other hand, are ideal for travel or testing a new formula before committing. You’ll also want to consider what you shave.

I rock a beard most of the time, so I only shave for touch-ups on my neck and cheeks. Plus, I rarely shave body hair and stick to trimming. Because of this, I can often get away with a smaller tube. But if you’re clean-cut or shave large parts of your body, you’ll want to look to larger options.

We’ve been testing razors since 2018, and naturally, every swipe meant testing the shaving creams that make them glide, too. For this update, I considered old favorites and new offerings from brands I trust to find the best-performing creams on the market. After over a year of testing (and plenty of shaves), I narrowed dozens down to 15 top contenders. I then evaluated or reevaluated each formula for cushion, glide, price, and how well it prevented irritation. After all that lathering, these seven shaving creams earned the title of best in 2026.

#5000. The Best Epilators for At-Home Hair Removal in 2026, According to Experts

Here's why they're better than waxing, shaving, or a laser.

Fall’s signature cool, crisp temperatures have me reevaluating more than just my wardrobe. My skincare routine is due for a seasonal refresh—but one beauty ritual that I won’t skip is body hair removal. There’s nothing wrong with body hair, of course. But if you’re like me and prefer smooth, dolphin-like skin brushing against your matching workout sets and cozy sweater dresses, then chances are that you’ve tried a slew of hair removal methods.

Shaving is cheap and easy, but it requires daily maintenance. Depilatory hair removal creams are convenient, but they can easily irritate sensitive skin. Waxing results last up to six weeks, but the discomfort can also be unpleasant for those with sensitive skin. Some of our editors adore laser hair removal devices, but they’ll set you back at least $300. Many aren’t designed with Brown and Black skin tones like mine.

However, we’re all in on one hair removal technique: epilators. They resemble electric razors, but instead of trimming hairs at the surface, they pluck them from the root for long-lasting, smooth skin. Because the hair-free results last for two to four weeks, epilators are a great alternative to shaving and hair removal creams. Repeated sessions slow down hair growth, and your unwanted strands will be finer when they regrow, says dermatologist Hadley King, MD. They’re also gentler than laser hair removal devices, which is why Dr. King recommends them for anyone with sensitive skin or who isn't a good fit for laser hair removal.

My favorites start at just $9, so you can enjoy hair-free skin without putting a major dent in your beauty budget ahead of the holiday season. Plus, many of our recommendations are sold on Amazon, meaning you can take full advantage of the retailer’s signature two-day Prime shipping and enjoy hair-free legs before your upcoming weekend plans.

WH editors haven’t met a Braun device we don’t love—and this top-rated epilator is no exception. I love that it’s equipped with a wide, flexible head that flawlessly bends along the curves of my kneecaps, underarms, and my bikini line. Even better? It features an impressive number of micro-grip tweezers, which are much slimmer than traditional tweezers in the motor to ensure I get the closest hair removal possible. While it sounds intimidating, the sheer number of tweezers sped up my hair removal process.

This wet-dry device has an impressive 50-minute runtime which allows me to remove unwanted body hair over several sessions without worrying about it dying mid-epilating. It also has a relatively quick charging time of just an hour, which is shorter than other epilators I’ve come across in my research and testing process.

Despite the lightweight feel, I like how sturdy this device is and that it doesn’t easily slip out of my grip. Plus, it's waterproof so you can use your new epilator in the shower without worrying about it cranking out mid-shave.

And while a small detail, this device has a built-in “smartlight” that illuminates your skin while epilating, solidifying it as a must-have for women who like dimmer lighting while showering but still want to see what they're doing.

Truthfully, the only bummer about this device is that it’s the most expensive recommendation. However, we think its performance makes it worth it.

Love the idea of a facial epilator but you don’t need the face cleansing brush or facial toning attachments? Reach for this $21 find from Remington. The only downside with this device is that it can only be used dry, so it’s best to use after cleansing your face.

If you need razor-sharp precision, this device has the smallest head on the list. It’s designed to quickly, safely, and easily pluck away multiple stray hairs in your eyebrow area. You can still use this on your face, lips, chin, and even nose, but it’ll just take a little longer because the tip is so small. So what makes this sub-$40 epilator worth it? Thanks to interchangeable heads, you can epilate, trim, and shave with a single device. You can use the gentle trimmer to cut down longer body hairs, an epilator to remove them from the root, and the shaver attachment to clean up any areas when you’re in a pinch. Swapping out the attachments is seamless—and the shaver is awesome for days I want smooth skin, but my body hair isn't long enough for epilating.

Beginners will especially love the trimmer because it doesn't irritate our sensitive skin. And the epilator head has a built-in massage roller that helps minimize any discomfort. While it's not as effective as our best overall epilator, it gets the job done by removing all of our unwanted body hair in around 30 minutes. Most importantly, the pain is rather minimal. Not too shabby for a compact, travel-friendly pick!

The biggest downside with this tool is that it’s not designed to remove unwanted facial hair. That said, you can pluck away rogue chin hairs or reach for the Amazon bestselling Kitsch dermaplaning tool that trims your brows and shaves your face to reveal smoother skin.

Epilators are unique because they’re equipped with built-in tweezers to pluck hairs from the root.

The smaller heads have fewer tweezers, but they're fantastic for targeted areas like the face, underarms, and bikini line.

Larger epilator heads are better for covering bigger areas like your legs. Having a lot of tweezers helps speed up your hair removal routine, but it also means you’ll have a more painful experience because it’s plucking dozens of hairs at a time. But like ripping a bandage off a hairy arm, it’s uncomfortable at first, but not too rough. And FWIW, Dr. King promises the pain level noticeably improves after multiple sessions. So be brave and patient, and it’ll all be over before you know it.

For the most effective hair removal, your body hair should be about the length of a sprinkle or grain of rice (about 0.25 inches or 6.35 mm). This standard for epilators is the same as waxing and sugaring. When your hair is too short, it's challenging for the epilator to grasp and remove the strands. You also don't want them to be longer than about two rice grains to help prevent hairs from getting tangled and minimize pain. Everyone's hair regrowth is different, but for most people, stubble typically occurs within one to two weeks.

It sounds like a small detail, but also consider the power source.

If you have minimal outlets in your home, then battery-powered makes sense. However, the hidden cost of replacing batteries can start to add up within the year. That said, all of the featured battery-operated devices in this story include a battery to help offset the long-term cost.

These devices are great because you won’t have to worry about them cranking out mid-epilating, but honestly the cords can get in the way. If you’ve got the extra funds, it’s best to invest in a cordless device so you can remove your unwanted body hair without stretching in odd positions or sitting on your bedroom floor. That said, there are some stellar corded options, including the relatively affordable $40 Philips Epilator Series 2000.

Water-resistant devices can be used wet or dry, so the cordless option can be used in your shower and the corded version works on your damp body if you prefer. Most aren’t waterproof, except the Braun Epilator Silk-épil 9 Flex 9-481 Beauty Set and the epilator head on the Colordiary Eyebrow Hair Remover.

As our beauty editor, I’m constantly on the hunt for the best products, and spend the vast majority of my time testing and reviewing the latest drops. I also regularly consult dermatologists about all things beauty, which is exactly what I did to kick off the selection process for our best epilators story. After talking with Dr. King (she’s one of my most trusted dermatological experts), I asked about her recommendations and insights into shopping for epilators. Then, our team tested several of her picks and compared them to some of the other epilators in our beauty closet.

We've been testing epilators since March 2021, and over time we've evaluated dozens of newer models with various features until we settled on these seven winners. In the years since, we've kept a close eye on the latest launches across all price points and have updated this story at least yearly to share our honest thoughts. For our most recent update, we tried 12 epilators and determined these seven are worthy of a place in our routine—and we're confident they'll equally impress you as well.

Over the last six weeks we've been trying a slew of options and kept the number of tweezers, power source, and water resistance in mind. Next, we paid attention to the number of attachments. We prioritized accessories that helped alleviate discomfort to ensure we have less intimidating options for beginners. Next, we considered each epilator's ease of use, noise level, grip strength, comfort, and efficacy at removing hair. Our team used these devices in our real lives and ahead of important events, like weddings, birthdays, and after exercise.

To narrow down the list even further, I recruited Women's Health colleagues, including Assistant Social Media Editor Isabel McMahon, to join the testing process. I also carefully vetted all of the top-rated picks across Amazon, Ulta, and Sephora. I also considered pricing. While yes, the top pick is over $250, it’s from Braun, one of the most-trusted names in the hair removal game. It also earned major snaps from McMahon and me. And FWIW, our other picks are $140 and under, with some in the sweet $10-$40 range.

If you’re interested in giving epilating a shot, the above are some highly reviewed options that will get you on your way to smooth, bare skin.

These devices look like chunky electric razors and are either manual like a traditional women’s razor or powered by batteries or an electrical outlet. When you run the device across your body, tiny tweezers pluck away unwanted body hair. So yes, the initial hair removal process will be a tad uncomfy, but the smooth results are so worth it, says Dr. King.

Like all other hair removal techniques, using an epilator is all about skin prep. Dr. King recommends a gentle physical exfoliation, such as a body scrub, gloves, mitt, loofah, or brush, before epilation. (Psst: I’ve been using Nécessaire The Body Exfoliant since 2019 and haven’t looked back since.) "This will help to expose hairs so they can be picked up by the epilator, and it also helps decrease the risk of ingrown hairs," says Dr. King.

#4995. The 6 Best Undereye Patches, Tested and Reviewed by Dermatologists and Beauty Editors

The entire Women's Health team swears by them.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’m always up late doomscrolling TikTok and The White Lotus subreddit for season 4 theories. (Natasha Rothwell hive, stand up!) The only problem? Those late nights mean I have dark circles and puffiness in the morning (boo!). While I'm a huge fan of undereye creams, sometimes I get bored and need to switch things up. Enter undereye patches. They're a fast fix for dryness, puffiness, and dark circles—and even help me fake eight hours of sleep. "The skin under the eyes is prone to changes related to aging skin, such as fine lines, and conditions like dryness and discoloration," says dermatologist Brendan Camp, MD. In just 10 to 20 minutes, undereye patches temporarily hydrate the delicate skin and help me look refreshed. Plus, they're super cute and add a fun touch to my selfies, even if they're shared to just my Close Friends circle on Instagram Stories.

Like any other skin care product, eye masks really get their power from their ingredients, some of which are typically hyaluronic acid, vitamin C, niacinamide, and caffeine.

“Eye patches incorporate key ingredients like hyaluronic acid to boost moisture, peptides to firm, ceramides to strengthen the skin barrier, caffeine to help reduce puffiness, and niacinamide to reduce discoloration,” says dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD.

As with any beauty product, there are always a few things to consider before making the investment. Since these masks are mostly advertised for their ability to soothe and hydrate, you'll want to check the hydrating and firming ingredients, and keep your expectations realistic since results are usually temporary. Here's what to look out for.

For starters, look for key ingredients such as aloe, chamomile, cucumber, green tea, glycerin, or hyaluronic acid. You're less likely to come across vitamin C and retinol, but it's a plus if you do. Patches with a cellulose gel material can also prevent them from sliding off your face (a con I often deal with and try to avoid as much as possible).

Not only is the skin under your eyes thinner and more delicate than in other areas of your face, but it’s also where lymphatic fluid drainage occurs, says dermatologist Lauren Penzi, MD. It can also show more blood vessels, and in turn, make dark circles appear more visible, says Dr. Garshick. Most eye masks are created to reduce fine lines, undereye darkness, and wrinkles while giving your skin the boost of moisture it needs. The overall effect of these patches is to revive and hydrate, which is why so many people use them to get a more refreshed look.

Many people complain about looking tired, and eye patches are a nice, quick fix. Still, it's important to be realistic about the kind of results you'll get in just one or two uses. So, you’ll want to zero in on the reason you’re buying patches, says Dr. Camp. For example, you can target puffiness by rocking undereye patches infused with caffeine or green tea while getting ready for work, says Dr. Camp.

As a member of the beauty team at Women’s Health, I’m constantly on the hunt for the best products and spend a lot of my time testing and reviewing the latest drops. I frequently consult skin experts, which is exactly what I did to kick off my selection process here. I consulted five New York-based dermatologists and had them give their recommendations with insight on why these undereye masks are so splurge-worthy. Then, I tested several of their picks and compared them to some of the other undereye masks available in our beauty closet.To narrow down the list even further, I got a few other members of team WH, including Addison Aloian, Lily Wohlner, Brian Underwood, and Danielle Jackson, to get in on the testing process. Ingredients, price, and overall efficacy were taken into account to determine which would be best for a wide range of needs and preferences.Here are the fruits of our labor.

After testing tons of undereye masks, this one takes the cake for best overall. Why? It's the most hydrating option on this list and it doesn't slip off your face, which is super hard to find in an undereye mask.

ICYMI, Wander Beauty basically started the undereye mask trend. This OG mask is made with peptides, amino acids, and hyaluronic acid to improve your skin's texture, tone, and hydration. It's also expert-approved by Dr. Garshick and dermatologist Dendy Engelman, MD. "I love that this mask is made with three different layers that allow the formula to penetrate the skin deeply and prevent it from sliding off the face, so you can multitask while you wear it," says Dr. Engelman.

Wander Beauty patches are as effective as they are Instagrammable. I’ve been a fan of the rose gold and yellow gold patches for five years, and all of my beauty editor friends gush over them. They brighten, hydrate, and plump up my fine lines. They also contain calendula extract and aloe vera to help reduce puffiness. Ahem, hi holiday parties and upcoming travel—I’m looking at you.

These pretty patches have three unique layers: the surface's foil retains heat and prevents evaporation, the middle grips to prevent slippage, and the base delivers moisturizing glycerin and depuffing calendula extract. For an extra soothing experience, I like to leave mine in the fridge. Cool temperatures help shrink blood vessels under the eyes, so dark circles appear lighter and puffiness minimizes, dermatologist Marisa Garshick, MD, said in our guide to undereye skin care.

That said, the construction of this mask consists of super light and flexible material versus the conventional plastic material found in a lot of other eye patches that were tested, giving this product a high-quality feel.

I would be remiss if I didn't mention my personal fave patch from Patchology. It contains hyaluronic acid (hi, hydrated, plump skin) and feels super cool under the eyes to de-puff and smooth out that area.

Patchology is fantastic for targeting lines, says dermatologist Anar Mikailov, MD. He mentions that there's resveratrol, a natural antioxidant found in grapes that helps improve barrier function, and other antioxidants that provide protection against oxidizing agents that can visibly age the skin by causing wrinkles. There’s also antioxidant-rich strawberry extract, which helps brighten dark circles.

After using this patch, I also noticed my undereye area was less puffy and more luminous. My only con was that the mask slides out of place after a while, but it’s still epic to use and totally worth incorporating into your routine. My hack is to use these patches while lying down in bed to prevent any slipping.

This undereye mask is basically an expert at reducing puffy, tired-looking eyes thanks to its cooling effects. It also temporarily plumps up my fine lines with hydrating hyaluronic acid.

This option comes with a lot of serum, so it may slip down your face over time. But, feel free to go ahead and massage that extra serum into your undereye area—that little bit of massaging can help assist with lymphatic drainage and further reduce puffiness. Need even more convincing? Celebs like Jessica Alba post about this mask on her Instagram story time and time again, noting that she's a major fan.

Most masks on this list only need 10 minutes on the skin, but this one should stay on for up to 20. Although, 20 minutes fly by when you have a good book in hand (pro tip!).

These eye masks from Live Tinted are packed with copper peptides and banana extract (hi, Ashton Hall!) to reduce puffiness and smooth fine lines. They also reduce puffiness after just a few uses and leave skin looking glowy and feeling hydrated.

And because these patches help soften and smooth your delicate undereye area, Aloian relies on them for makeup prep. "Not only is the patch super cute—it's shaped like a sun—but it also genuinely hydrates and brightens my undereye area," she says. These patches make Aloian feel confident going makeup free because of the glow they leave behind, but it's just as helpful on days when she wants a dewy base before applying concealer.

Along with a mix of peptides to help stimulate collagen production, this eye mask contains niacinamide, bakuchiol, caffeine, and vitamin C. Bakuchiol is a great retinol alternative that helps stimulate collagen production, says Dr. Mikailov.

Wohlner also gave this patch a try and loves how flexible it is under the eye. However, she did note that it does tend to slip down the face because it's super thin.

This vitamin C-packed eye patch is perfect for helping brighten up the undereye area while reducing signs of aging and puffiness with the help of caffeine.

Yeah, it's a little pricier, but trust that it's totally worth it if you have the budget. The gel patches are super easy to apply. Plus, they can reduce discoloration and fine lines within just a few weeks. Sometimes I'm wary of products with vitamin C in them because the smell can be a bit aggressive, but these are just right.

Derms also deem this patch worth the money. "The key ingredient in this mask is THD Ascorbate Vitamin C, which is 50 times more powerful than other forms of vitamin C," says Dr. Engelman. THD is especially good for surface dark spots that need brightening rather than deeper dark circles, says Dr. Mikailov.

It's worth noting that these dry up around the 10-minute mark, and while they stay on really well, the edges break off easily if you try to move the masks around a few minutes after the initial application.

As the name suggests, this patch is meant to soothe tired-looking eyes. So, for those of you who have a lot of sleepless nights or are just night owls at heart, this is your winner. Infused with caffeine, niacinamide, and hyaluronic acid, these work overtime to reduce puffiness and dark circles.

"I often recommend Peace Out’s acne patch for the face, but I also love the brand’s eye patches," says Dr. Engelman. "It's so effective at quickly bringing down puffiness and brightening and smoothing the under-eyes." The patch is biodegradable and made with biocellulose, which helps the formula deeply penetrate the skin, says Dr. Engelman.

These patches fit snugly under my eyes, so I could wear them while doing my eye makeup. They also did a great job of catching eyeshadow fallout that would normally ruin my undereye concealer. Another pro? Unlike most gel patches, they weren’t completely soaked in serum, which can make the process a bit messy. Instead, they had just the right amount for ample hydration. After the initial use, I noticed my undereyes were softer and brighter, and I’d slowly reach for these patches for special occasions.

I’m not the only fan on WH’s beauty team. “I have very sensitive skin, so I'm always cautious when it comes to trying things out, but this didn't give me any issues,” says tester Sabrina Talbert. “It also doesn't have much of a scent, which put my mind at ease since fragrance tends to be an early indicator that my skin might not like a product.”

These patches are on the larger side, so they feel a bit bulky. They also need to be slightly adjusted because they slide down a little bit over 15 minutes, but honestly, they’re such minor cons that Talbert continues using them.

#4994. Muhammad Ali at Home: 10 Photos of the Heavyweight Champion’s Life Outside the Ring

It was a stroke of luck—bad luck—that got Muhammad Ali into the ring for the first time. The Louisville, Kentucky, native was 12 years old when his brand-new bicycle was stolen. The police officer to whom Ali reported the theft happened to own a boxing gym—and became his first coach.

Ten years later, in 1964, Ali, then still known by his birth name, Cassius Clay, became the world heavyweight champion when he defeated reigning titleholder Sonny Liston. The athlete, who earned the nickname “The Greatest,” would go on to win that title two more times, as well as an Olympic gold medal and numerous honors for his civil rights activism and humanitarian work.

There was, of course, another side to the legend: his domestic life. As we gear up for the release of the Prime Video series The Greatest, which explores the prizefighter’s rise to prominence, we’re looking back at photos of Ali in his off-duty hours.

Days after becoming the heavyweight champion, Ali announced his conversion to the Nation of Islam, changed his name, and then relocated to Chicago, where the controversial religion’s headquarters are based. (He later converted to Sunni Islam). In 1967, Ali cited his religious beliefs when he refused to serve in the US Army during the Vietnam War. His boxing license revoked and his championship title stripped, Ali entered a period of exile. He is pictured in his Chicago home the following year, reading a book by Nation of Islam leader Elijah Muhammad. The athlete shared the dwelling with his second wife, Khalilah Camacho-Ali, whom he married at the residence on August 17, 1967. The single-story brick house was in the Avalon Park neighborhood and was a fully furnished gift from the Nation of Islam.

The boxer and his toddler Maryum feeding 10-week-old twins Rasheda and Jamillah in their Philadelphia home.

The couple welcomed a daughter, Maryum, in 1968, and two years later, twins named Rasheda and Jamillah. The newborns are pictured between Ali and Maryum at home in Pennsylvania in this November 1970 photograph. The fighter and his family stayed at the home, in West Philadelphia’s Overbrook Park neighborhood, for about a year. It was later owned by Kobe Bryant’s grandparents.

Ali with fans at his Pennsylvania training camp in August 1974.

Though he soon relocated to New Jersey, Ali would maintain ties to Pennsylvania for decades with his training camp, Fighter’s Heaven. He purchased the Deer Lake property in 1972, the year after the Supreme Court overturned his draft-evasion conviction, allowing him to regain his boxing license. On the land, he custom-built a log gym, a dining hall, several cabins, a mosque, and a courtyard with a large stone fireplace. His training sessions were open to the public; in this August 1974 photo, a group of fans are pictured behind him at the camp. He kept the retreat long after his retirement, selling it in 1997 to martial arts instructor George Dillman. The property is now a tourist destination, complete with a small museum.

Ali at home in Los Angeles before his fight with Larry Holmes.

Ali briefly retired from boxing at age 37 in 1979, but returned the following year to fight Larry Holmes. The boxer poses at his home office in Hancock Park, Los Angeles, in this August 1980 photo, taken about a month before his fight with Holmes.

Ali shoots pool in his Hancock Park house in this 1980 photo.

Ali shows off the game room in his Hancock Park, Los Angeles, home in this 1980 snapshot. Around this period, he started to show early symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, which impacted his athletic ability. He lost the fight to Holmes and went back into retirement.

The boxing champion and his wife Veronica at home in 1982.

In 1981, Ali fought one last time before hanging up his gloves. “I know it’s the end,” he said after losing the fight. “I’m not crazy. After Holmes, I had excuses. I was too light. Didn’t breathe right. No excuses this time. I’m happy. I’m still pretty. I could have a black eye. Broken teeth. Split lips. I think I came out all right for an old man.” Ali stands next to his third wife, Veronica Porché, in front of his Hancock Park dwelling in this photo, taken a few months after his final match.

The Greatest takes a call at home in 1982.

In this photo from the same March 1982 photo shoot, Ali strikes a pose in his opulent Los Angeles living room. The retired boxer had purchased the 14,500-square-foot home in 1979, two years after marrying Porché. The 1916 build, by architect John C. Austin, was an Italian Renaissance mansion complete with seven bedrooms.

The estate featured stained glass window panels designed by Louis Comfort Tiffany (the son of Tiffany & Co. founder Charles Lewis Tiffany) and a stately dining room with intricately carved dark wood and a crystal chandelier, as seen in this October 1985 photo of Ali eating cereal. That year, he and Porché filed for divorce.

Ali outfitted the home with a (packed) trophy room, which he shows off in this 1985 picture. He left the Hancock Park dwelling the following year, when his and Porché’s divorce was finalized. Shortly after, Ali married his fourth wife, Lonnie Williams. As his Parkinson’s disease progressed (he was officially diagnosed in 1984), Williams became Ali’s primary caregiver.

The former fighter has his picture taken by photographer Neil Leifer at home in Arizona’s Paradise Valley.

Ali poses for a photo shoot commemorating his 70th birthday in 2012 at the Arizona home he and Williams shared. That year, he was honored with the Liberty Medal for his humanitarian efforts, which he devoted more time to following his retirement. He was also awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005. Ali died in Arizona in 2016 at 74.

#4991. 12 Health Benefits of Pilates That Make It Worth the Hype, According to a Physical Therapist

Say hello to core strength, better endurance, and less back pain.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s a reason Pilates has a reputation of being a leg-shaking, muscle-quaking workout. But it’s more than just a hard workout—it ended up being a total game changer for my health.

As an orthopedic physical therapist and conditioning coach, I’ve built my life around strength, health, and movement. Sports have always been central to who I am—running, weightlifting, and higher-intensity training used to be my norm—though my body hasn’t always kept up.

Then, last summer, I took my first reformer Pilates class at Bodyrok, a 45-minute full-body group fitness class. It was humbling—I engaged muscles I rarely worked in traditional strength training sessions (hello, core) and tackled moves I had never done before. But slowing down and focusing on controlled movements also felt surprisingly satisfying.

After eight months of consistent reformer Pilates classes (plus running and strength training sessions), I finally understood the hype. It has strengthened my core and pelvic muscles, improved circulation to alleviate pain, and eased inflammation. Plus, it complements my sport performance because it targets stabilizer muscles and mobility.

Here’s why both mat and reformer Pilates truly deliver, according to research.

Of all the benefits Pilates offers, it’s most famous for its focus on core strength—a key foundation for nearly everything we do, from lifting a baby and swinging a golf club to simply maintaining good posture at a desk. More specifically, Pilates targets the deep stabilizing muscles of the core, including the often overlooked transverse abdominis, as well as the rectus abdominis, or your six-pack muscles.

Want to pair Pilates and strength training in a streamlined way? Try the Women’s Health+ Pilates x Lift workout plan, a four-week program that gives you the best of both modalities to build muscle, improve mobility, and protect your joints.

Pilates combines controlled movements that lengthen and stretch your muscles, helping improve flexibility and range of motion within a joint. In fact, just six weeks of Pilates may improve functional mobility, according to research in the Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies. By working your muscles through their full range of motion, Pilates makes everyday activities like climbing stairs and bending down to tie your shoes feel easier and more fluid.

Most of us spend hours hunched over computers, then move straight to our phones or the TV, which can wreak total havoc on our posture. Fortunately, Pilates can undo those habits by strengthening the core and upper back, stabilizing the shoulders, and opening up the chest.

Research supports these benefits: A 2024 systematic review published in Archives of Rehabilitation Research and Clinical Translation found that after eight weeks of Pilates, sedentary women showed improvements in both posture and their ability to perform daily activities. Pilates also emphasizes proper form and alignment, so you’re constantly practicing better posture during your workouts—a habit that, with practice, can naturally carry over into everyday life.

Pilates isn’t just about your core—it’s a full-body workout that fires up multiple muscle groups at once, building strength from head to toe, especially when using a reformer for added resistance. In fact, a 2025 randomized trial published in Nature found that women who practiced reformer Pilates for 60 minutes three times per week for eight weeks saw measurable gains in muscle mass, grip strength, and body composition.

Research also shows that Pilates can boost muscular endurance, or the ability of your muscles to perform repeated contractions or maintain a position against resistance over time.

What truly sets Pilates apart, though, is its focus on the smaller stabilizing muscles most people ignore, which play a key role in controlled, efficient movement. Because of this, Pilates can enhance functional movement patterns, making it a secret weapon for better performance and fewer injuries.

The functional strength and stability aspects of Pilates make it an excellent complement to heavy lifting (which you should still do two to three times a week to develop bone density, improve metabolic health, and develop muscular power). That’s because a strong core protects against injury (like lower back pain) and helps you maintain good form even when handling a heavy barbell, per 2023 research in Healthcare.

Pilates is all about syncing breath, focus, and fluid movement, encouraging a deep connection between the mind and body. Each exercise requires careful attention to form, encouraging intentional, controlled movement that can feel almost meditative. This mindfulness, combined with the focus on strengthening the mind-body connection (the two-way link between your mental state and physical health), naturally supports mental well-being.

Because breathing is central to Pilates, it can also reduce stress and promote a sense of calm. As a matter of fact, doing Pilates just once a week for an hour over the span of three months can improve anxiety, depression, and stress, according to 2025 research in Healthcare.

About 80 percent of adults in the U.S. will experience lower back pain at some point in their lives, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH). But Pilates can help relieve that pain, as it stabilizes the core and improves posture, according to a 2025 study in the Irish Journal of Medical Science. The study had 66 participants ages 18 to 65 with lower back pain either do Pilates three times a week or a home exercise program (involving stretching, strengthening, and mobility exercises) for eight weeks. The group that did Pilates experienced improvements in pain relief, functional disability, and quality of life, compared to those who did the home exercise program.

Additionally, a 2022 review in the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy looked at 118 trials to find out the best exercise options for reducing pain and disability in adults with chronic lower back pain. It looked at aerobic, strength, combined aerobic and strength, core-based, McKenzie (movements designed to relieve musculoskeletal pain), Pilates, stretching, and mind-body exercise. It found that Pilates, core-based, and mind-body exercise were the best for reducing pain—but Pilates had the highest likelihood for lowering pain and disability.

Your balance decreases as you age, according to the NIH, but not if you do something about it. A 2021 study in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health observed the effects of Pilates training on balance and fall risk in older women. It had 50 women over 60 years old either do two Pilates sessions for three months, or no exercise outside of everyday activities. Before and after training, the women did exercises like the single-leg stance and Timed Up and Go (where you stand from a sitting position, walk, and then do it in reverse), and other tests. The group that did Pilates improved their balance and lowered their fall risk more than the group that didn’t exercise.

One 2021 review of literature on exercise and longevity in Aging shows how regular exercise can slow down cellular aging—and Pilates is a great fitness modality to support strength, mobility, and confidence as we age. Since it’s low-impact and lower intensity, it can help build strength without overstressing your joints, making it a sustainable workout for now and the future.

In fact, in a 2025 study in the Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies, 24 adults age 76, on average, either did 20 weeks of an online Pilates program or no exercise. Their balance, core stability, and functional fitness were tested with exercises like the single-leg stance, 6-minute walk test, and core muscle strength and stability tests. The study found that the Pilates program improved balance, cardiorespiratory endurance, and core strength in older adults, especially compared to the group that didn’t exercise.

Both mat and reformer Pilates can provide all of the benefits above, but they also have some of their own distinct draws. Reformer Pilates, specifically, can be really useful for training muscle patterns in a gentle way—by using springs for resistance rather than gravity, WH previously reported. (Think: footwork while lying down on a reformer rather than a standing squat with a barbell.) As a result, you’re able to relax more into each move, making it a lower-impact workout.

And with its moving carriage, the Pilates reformer can be a valuable tool for building greater balance and stability, as it creates a greater challenge than you’d get on solid ground with a mat workout.

What’s more, a reformer can help support someone rehabbing from an injury—particularly because it can help correct misaligned movement patterns more effectively than simply completing a bodyweight move.

Perhaps the best part of any Pilates modality? It’s for anyone and everyone, no matter your age or fitness level. While some Pilates classes (i.e., those using reformers) can be intimidating and costly, you actually don’t need any equipment to get started. Pilates can be done with just your body and a workout mat, and you can even replicate reformer-style moves using sliders, foam rollers, and towels.

No matter how you practice, the focus on controlled movement and mindful breathing makes Pilates a real game changer for athletic performance and holistic wellness. Trust me, I speak from experience.

#4989. This DC Designer’s Nearly 200-Year-Old Virginia Farmhouse Flourishes With Detail and History

In the foothills of Virginia’s Blue Ridge Mountains, just minutes from Shenandoah National Park, the town of Sperryville (population: 350) still feels like a well-kept secret. In recent years, it’s attracted the eye of Washington, DC–based designer Melissa Colgan of Melissa Colgan Interiors, who purchased a weekend home there in 2023.

Though born in the Midwest, the designer and her husband, Daniel Schned, moved to DC in 2016 and spent their early years and weekends exploring the surrounding countryside. “One of the areas we fell in love with is Rappahannock County,” she says of discovering its scenic pastures, rolling hills, and grazing cows. “It feels a world away from DC.”

The staircase is covered in Schumacher’s Caterpillar Leaf print and the stair runner is by Sinclair Till. The cloche is custom by Dan Nakamura.

In the family room, the BDDW sofa is upholstered in a Décors Barbares fabric. The side table is from Covesville Antiques and topped with a lamp by Christopher Spitzmiller. The artwork is by Molly van Amerongen.

The fruitwood dining table from 1stDibs is surrounded with chairs by Lorenzo Castillo and upholstered in a fabric by Schumacher. The 1930s chandelier has custom shades covered in a Decors Barbares fabric. The chairs are by Leah O’Connell (left) and Soane. The artwork is by Joshua Perkin.

In 2020, the couple eloped at The Inn at Little Washington and began looking for a vacation home in the area. Three years later, they found a listing for an 1830s farmhouse and barn, which happened to be the former home and office of the county doctor. “It’s a very special house in Sperryville because it’s where the doctor saw all his patients in the early 1900s,” Colgan says.

What began as an 1830s single-room log cabin evolved to include a barn and second story in the 1890s, followed by another addition in the late 1990s. “A lot of the original details were still there,” Colgan says of the 1,200-square-foot residence. “We just wanted to freshen things up a bit.”

In the family living room, the windows, along with the original chink log siding, date to the 1830s. “I wanted to lean into some of the depth that was already there,” Colgan says of her color palette. “That prompted me into the world of deep reds, ochres, and blues.”

In a cozy corner, a Casamidy chair covered in soft mohair flanks a Swedish Gustavian oak secretary from the 1800s.

Colgan solicited the help of DC architect Alexander Smith of Mortar & Thatch. “The thing we aligned with from the very beginning is we didn't want it to feel like a new renovation,” Smith says. “Maybe we slapped on some paint or got new countertops, but we didn’t want it to seem like we were implanting foreign ideas.”

The biggest task was subdividing the single bedroom upstairs to accommodate Colgan’s growing family. At the time, she was pregnant with her now two-year-old daughter. “We basically took down the walls of the one bedroom, made a middle bedroom for our daughter, then eked every inch we could in order to fit a king bed and built-in closets in our room,” she says. The result is a quaint and colorful two-bedroom blueprint, with dappled light dancing through the street-facing windows.

In the pocket-size half bath, an American Federal mahogany mirror broadens the space, which is wrapped in Iksel Mogul Berry Wallpaper by Schumacher and adorned with an oil painting by Jay Harper.

Incorporating open shelves in the kitchen helped maximize storage while enabling the designer to showcase more of the home’s attractive chink log siding. Farrow & Ball’s Terre de Egypte paint accentuates Colgan’s collections of splatterware mugs and vintage objects, like an early-20th-century painter’s palette.

Today, they spend most of their time in the living room downstairs, with its original chink log siding from the 1830s. “The room is so soulful. You just walk in and take a deep breath,” she says. “The thing that came to mind early on was a little Russian country house or dacha. When we first saw the listing, we were in Switzerland, so that was the original seed for the design.”

Drawing from the warmth and depth of the living room’s original pine floors and log siding, Colgan conjured a rich color palette of ochres, reds, and blues with botanical and floral-patterned fabrics that mirrored the pastoral landscape. “We’re surrounded by mountains and flora and fauna, so I wanted the house to reflect that as well.”

A brisbee curtain in Lake August’s flowering Nasturtium fabric adds light and whimsy to the kitchen’s neutral cabinetry.

The kitchen pendants are by Urban Electric. The walls are painted in Dimity and the cabinets are painted Joa’s White, both by Farrow & Ball. The rug is by Matt Camron.

The furnishings are an array of old, new, and local finds from their 1920s French fruitwood dining table to the early American rocking chair salvaged from Ruckersville Antiques. “We didn’t really have anything for this house because the style is so different from our city home, so we had to start from scratch,” Colgan says. Still, the designer is an avid collector and had some pieces sitting in storage like the BDDW sofa, purchased at auction, that’s now in her living room. Currently, it’s upholstered in Décors Barbares’ lively Roses Tchékhonine print, with winged butterflies flitting across a canvas of cobalt and crimson flowers.

In the primary bedroom, every inch mattered. “We did multiple layouts and wanted to make sure the details, finishes, and everything in there was an appropriate scale so things didn’t feel too big or too small for the space,” says Smith. The walls and his-and-her closets are painted in Farrow & Ball’s Pink Ground and Eating Room Red, with Roman shades done in a Lucrezia fabric by Fortuny. An acrylic and ink work on paper by artist Julie Wolfe, which Colgan gave to her husband for their first wedding anniversary, hangs over the bed.

In the sunlit bathroom, blue and white garden tiles from Marble Systems bloom alongside fittings by Waterworks, D Porthault patterned towels, and an antique French mirror, circa 1785.

Other spaces, like the mudroom and laundry located near the home’s side entrance, were made more welcoming and useful, with cupboards dressed in wholesome, hay-colored gingham skirts. Reconfiguring appliances and adding cabinets and open shelving helped optimize the kitchen’s storage and traffic flow. “We were able to inch out so much in such a small space,” Smith says.

Despite its demure size, the house today is a sensory retreat for the couple. “That first Thanksgiving was a real stress test,” Colgan says. The barn in the back, where the doctor kept his horse for making house calls across the county, was renovated by the previous owner to include a kitchenette, an open living room space, and sleeping quarters. “The barn had pigs in it up until the last owner, and he renovated it,” she says. “I’ve since layered in a lot of fabrics and antiques.”

In their daughter’s room, a late-19th-century faux-bamboo pine and bird’s eye maple bed is made up with D Porthault Pink Coeur’s linens and a one-of-a-kind PROJEKTITYYNY Wisteria baby quilt, stitched with Liberty fabrics. The bookshelf is from Crate & Barrel and the walls and windows are covered in Ottoline’s blue and brown Indian Tulip print.

The walls are covered in Caterpillar Leaf by Schumacher and the slipper chair is custom. The Roman shade is a fabric by Antoinette Poisson.

Off the home’s side entry, a laundry and mudroom papered in Beata Heuman’s Eyelash design is further brightened thanks to the café curtain and cabinet skirts in a jumbo gingham by Beata Heuman, finished with French grosgrain trim.

Ultimately, however, it was the historic farmhouse where Colgan concentrated her creative energy. “A lot of times people come into these old houses and instead of trying to think carefully about how to make modern life function there, they blow out walls and make everything open,” she says. Instead, she champions her home’s nuanced details, including planks of weathered wood that have patinated over time or the way sunlight shimmers off the 19th-century windows, with their panes of wavy glass. “They are very much not energy efficient,” she says, “but they are absolutely beautiful.”

The custom console is painted in Benjamin Moore’s Van Deusen Blue and the walls are covered in Beata Heuman’s Eyelash Spring. The 1960s mirror is from 1stDibs.

On the front porch, a five-piece set by Newell Jacobsen is upholstered in a sky-blue Lisa Fine Madras Performance fabric that complements the painted ceiling, and the neighbor’s vibrant home. “There are some fun houses on our street—the one across the street is yellow,” Colgan says. “I liked the idea of colors out there being a little brighter.”

#4988. sonnen files for insolvency in Germany as US sales double

Residential battery storage maker sonnen is reporting two very different stories today: Its German business has filed for insolvency, while sonnen USA says sales have doubled and it’s preparing to expand.

The insolvency filing comes just two months after Shell sold sonnen to investment group TIVEN. Germany’s Handelsblatt reported that sonnen GmbH confirmed the filing and informed roughly 400 employees in Wildpoldsried, Bavaria, on October 22.

For homeowners with sonnen batteries, the immediate question is what happens to service. According to Handelsblatt, the company intends to keep supporting its more than 150,000 existing customers. But a substantial overhaul is coming: Numerous subsidiaries are expected to be wound down or enter insolvency proceedings under self-administration, with only one production site remaining. The report does not identify that site.

Meanwhile, sonnen USA’s announcement describes a growing home battery business. The company says sales have doubled and production has tripled year over year, supported by expanded manufacturing in Stone Mountain, Georgia. It expects to deliver more than 180 megawatt-hours of residential battery storage in 2026.

Much of that growth comes from virtual power plants (VPPs). These connect home batteries so they can work together to support the grid, giving households another way to earn value from their solar and storage systems.

In Texas, sonnen says its SOLRITE offering serves more than 6,000 homes, combining rooftop solar, batteries, energy management, and VPP participation. In Massachusetts, its sonnenCommunity program offers cash rewards to participating homeowners in National Grid and Eversource territories. The company also reports rising sales through its Wattsmart program in Utah.

TIVEN bought the entire global business, including sonnen USA. US CEO Blake Richetta stated today that “TIVEN is firmly committed to the long-term success of sonnen USA as a strong, market-leading company in the North American VPP energy market.”

TIVEN stated that it “looks forward to bolstering the company’s impressive growth.”

But the US announcement leaves an important question unanswered: How will the German restructuring affect the US operation and its customers? It doesn’t address the insolvency filing, and sonnen USA declined to comment on developments in Germany when contacted by pv magazine.

The US growth figures show demand for sonnen’s batteries. What customers still need is a clear explanation of how manufacturing, software support, and service will be maintained through the restructuring.

#4987. What You Should Know About Exercising When Bone Density Is a Concern

Osteopenia or osteoporosis doesn’t have to sideline your workouts. Here’s what to do, how to modify, and when to back off.

You might have heard that being active is a good idea when you have osteopenia or osteoporosis, conditions marked by lower-than-normal bone density. But when you’re exercising specifically to improve bone health, some types of exercise may be more helpful than others. Before lacing up your sneakers, there are a few things to know.

“When patients ask me what they can do to preserve and protect their bone health, consistent weight bearing and resistance exercises are the first things I recommend,” says Nicole Leung, MD, director of the Osteoporosis and Bone Health Program at NYU Langone Health in New York City. “Bone is a living tissue, so it adapts to mechanical load through remodeling.”

When bone tissue is stressed via physical activity, your body responds by making more bone, helping strengthen the tissue. Exercise also lowers the activity of cells that dissolve and break down old bone. That combo helps preserve or even improve your bone mineral density, regardless of your health status. Exercise may slow or even prevent the progression of osteoporosis; if you have osteoporosis already, it can help you maintain the bone you have and reduce your risk for falls and fractures.

A bone-density diagnosis doesn’t mean you have to give up exercise—but your routine should reflect your fracture risk and health history. Here’s what Dr. Leung recommends for choosing activities, adapting your routine, and knowing when to check with your doctor before making major changes.

There are a few types of activities that make up a bone-friendly exercise plan, and it’s important to get the right amount of each. Here are the types of exercise to do regularly.

These are exercises where you’re on your feet and putting force on your muscles and bones as they work against gravity. Depending on factors like your age, fitness level, and bone mineral density, these activities can include:

People working to maintain their bone health should do these sorts of activities for 30 to 60 minutes, three to five days per week, according to the American College of Sports Medicine.

As for activities like swimming and cycling, they’re great for getting your heart pumping—but because they’re low-impact, they won’t do much for your bones. That said, feel free to do them in addition to your weight-bearing exercises if you enjoy them.

Lifting (relatively) heavy things works your muscles and helps build bone density. This includes free weights, machines, resistance bands, or body weight exercises like squats or push-ups. Aim for two to three strength sessions per week, and don’t be afraid to gradually go heavier (with your doctor’s okay). Pushing yourself to 70 to 90 percent of your max effort may deliver a bigger bone boost than lifting lighter weights, research suggests.

Having osteoporosis makes you more prone to fractures after falls, but you can strengthen your balance—and reduce your chances for a broken bone—with exercises like yoga, tai chi, or Pilates. “Any exercise where you have to shift your body weight side to side and forward and back can be very helpful for your stabilizing muscles,” Dr. Leung says. She recommends working balance exercises into your schedule a few times per week. Find safe modifications if you’re worried about falling, like holding onto a sturdy chair or touching a wall.

Whether you’ve been exercising for years, are just starting out, or are returning to a routine after a long hiatus, Dr. Leung advises paying attention to your posture, avoiding exercise when you’re overly exhausted, and increasing intensity gradually. Older women who are new to exercise can still do resistance training, she says, but may need to start at a slower pace and under supervision.

Despite the overall benefits of exercise, you still need to be careful, particularly when you have osteoporosis. Certain activities can set the stage for potential spine fractures, so before starting an exercise program, decide with your doctor or other qualified professional what is and isn’t safe for you.

According to the International Osteoporosis Foundation, you may need to limit or avoid moves that involve:

Yoga, while helpful for balance, can involve poses that put your spine at risk (like forward bends, deep twists, plow pose, shoulder stand, and pigeon pose). If you decide to give it a try, choose a class where the teacher can offer safe modifications, Dr. Leung says. It’s also best to steer clear of activities that come with a high risk of falling from above standing height, like skiing or horseback riding, she adds.

When it comes to stressing your bones, it’s possible to get too much of a good thing. “Overburdening your bone can actually lead to stress fractures,” Dr. Leung says. If you do prolonged intense weight-bearing and high-impact exercises like jogging or jumping rope, avoid scheduling them on back-to-back days. Alternate those workouts with activities like strength training, or have an active recovery day where you walk or do yoga or tai chi, she recommends.

Make it a point to stay active even after you’ve completed the day’s workout. According to Dr. Leung, non-exercise activities like casual walking or doing chores may help to maintain bone density when compared to sedentary behavior. Stroll over to chat with a coworker at their desk during a break, take the stairs when you can, or walk while you call a friend instead of sitting. A few minutes here and there can really add up.

Any new or worsening bone or spine pain is a warning sign to stop exercising and contact your doctor. You should also call your doctor if you fall while exercising, notice that you’ve had height loss, or if your spine appears curved, which could be signs of a spinal fracture. And always stop exercising and seek medical attention if you experience other severe symptoms like dizziness, faintness, or chest pain.

Consistency counts. People with low bone density who stay active over several months tend to see the greatest bone-health benefits, studies show. Choose activities you enjoy, build up gradually, and find a rhythm you can sustain. The goal isn’t to nail every workout—it’s to keep movement in your life.

#4985. Another megawatt-level charger enters China: 300 miles in 5 minutes

Chery has announced a 1.44 megawatt charging system, able to deliver 500km (311 miles) in 5 minutes. And it’s not even the fastest system available in China.

It’s become common knowledge at this point that Chinese EVs are the world’s state of the art, but the country isn’t sitting on its laurels, it’s still racing to compete with newer and better technology.

A case in point has been the country’s DC fast chargers, where we’ve seen a slew of announcements of new systems in just the last year.

BYD has a 1.5MW charger which it has already installed 10,000 of, Geely just announced a 2.2MW charger, and CATL has a hyper-fast charging battery.

The competition is so fierce that firms are starting to compete over seconds, not minutes of charging time.

And now, a new challenger appears: Chery.

Chery announced a 1.44MW charger that can add 500km (311miles) of range to a battery in 5 minutes, and can charge from 10-97% in 6 minutes and 50 seconds, as reported by CarNewsChina.

The numbers put it in league with the best of the best in the country. Per CarNewsChina’s accounting, the new Chery “Volt-Dragon” battery is the second-fastest at reaching 97% state of charge, 23 seconds behind CATL’s 6 minute, 27 second record time. FAW, Geely and BYD are all between 8 and 9 minutes for the same full charge metric.

Some other firms released times for charging in very cold or very warm weather, which Chery declined to release during its announcement. Though it did say that it could still deliver 500km of range in 8 minutes in “conservative scenarios.”

Could it be the drugged out Elon Musk is more into politics and taking over the world than advancing EV technology at an electric car company.

In Chery’s announcement, it dropped the same buzzword as Geely did: “AI-Powered.” Chery calls its system CheryMind, and supposedly it adjusts charging power based on temperature changes within the battery, to help maintain optimal charging speeds and battery health.

Meanwhile in the US, the fastest public chargers are around 400kW, with 750kW potentially coming next year. That’s all plenty quick enough for refueling, especially on a roadtrip, but for high-throughput DC charging locations, especially those in urban areas where some people might not have a consistent parking spot to charge in (and yes, we need to fix that), higher speed chargers can relieve a lot of pressure.

Chery has only just started installing chargers, and says it will have 100 chargers open in 10 Chinese cities soon. It plans to install 20,000 stations worldwide by 2029, which is quite a bit slower than BYD’s target to have 20,000 chargers installed by the end of this year.

#4984. 7 Pendant Lights to Perfect Your Overhead Lighting Scheme (2026)

Sure, recessed lighting serves a functional purpose, but pendant lights are where things get interesting. A quick sweep through any home tour, and you’ll recognize the strategically placed Louis Poulsen above the kitchen island, an Isamu Noguchi in the entryway, and a Herman Miller saucer pendant hovering over the living room that will steal the show. Below are seven pendant light fixtures that set the mood instead of harshening the vibe. We rounded up the best pendant lights for various design personalities, including a vintage-inspired showpiece and a few variations of low-key ambient lighting. Among them are most of the different types of pendant lights you’re likely to come across, with picks for modern minimalists, Belle Époque enthusiasts, and everyone in between.

First developed in 1958, the PH 5 is a classic for a reason. Renowned Danish lighting manufacturer Louis Poulsen designed the iconic pendant with a three-shade system to equally distribute light. While the pendant works for that functional purpose, it also doubles as an unconventional art piece. Choose from a number of monochromatic and multitone colorways, including this steel blue.

Look familiar? That’s because this large pendant, inspired by Noguchi’s Akaris, hangs in many an AD home tour, including above the dining room table in this Japandi-inspired Bay Area home and in the bedroom of this South African–inspired craft home, for example. There are a few reasons why this style of paper lighting is so popular: It goes with everything; it’s affordable; and it adds a sense of levity to the room with its ethereal shape and its soft, warm glow. As lantern pendants go, this option from Design Within Reach is about as low-commitment as they come. It works anywhere you want ambient lighting rather than a spotlight.

Designer pendant lights can cost upwards of $500, but you can pay a fraction of that with finds from Article, a direct-to-consumer furniture store that sells high-quality wares at more palatable prices. That’s certainly the case with the Aino pendant, with matte colorways and a simple angular silhouette that illuminates whatever you’re chef-ing up in your Scandi-style kitchen. The metal cone shade and braided fabric cord make it an easy pick for task lighting over a counter, and if you’re working with a tighter kitchen space, there’s also a mini pendant version for $99 that ships with an LED bulb.

This three-tiered ceiling light from West Elm adds visual texture to blank space, making it a welcome addition to transitional areas in need of personality. A piece like this can also help to add structure to an open plan where the kitchen and dining rooms collide. This piece comes in 26-inch and 32-inch sizes (the larger is a proper large pendant light that can hold its own over a dining table), as well as in hardwired and plug-in options, making it one of the few statement hanging lights you can install without calling an electrician.

Any cold kitchen space dominated by stone and steel fixtures could use a touch of handmade whimsy. Hanging this handwoven rattan pendant over a kitchen island promises to warm up the whole room. Usually, two or three pendant lights hang over a kitchen island; this single shade provides a cozy, welcoming alternative, softening the light rather than spotlighting the countertop, so your mise en place won’t feel so interrogated.

This midcentury Herman Miller pendant, aptly named a saucer for its elliptical shape, is prized by commerce writer Julia Harrison for its retro, Mad Men–esque appeal. Despite the resemblance to our Hay pick above, Miller wasn’t riffing on Noguchi with this pendant: He wanted a Swedish silk-covered pendant he couldn’t justify buying, so he made his own using a sprayed plastic skin originally developed for mothballing Navy ships (whereas the orbital Hay version uses rice paper). The vertical ribbing gives it a shape that seems to be almost expanding as it hangs. Its white shade and chrome hardware make it easily adaptable to many (if not most) design styles.

This lighting fixture brings to mind 10-foot ceilings, Flemish tapestries, and an echoey marble entryway. If you’re lucky enough to have all of the above, this is exactly the sort of pendant your space needs. If not, luckily, the fixture carries that whole vibe on its own, with its cream glass bowl, brass detailing, and a sculpted metal tassel that adds a bit of movement. A vintage-inspired piece like this transforms a more humble hallway into something dignified and scenic.

Ahead, three tried-and-true strategies for better, longer-lasting erections.

IF YOU HAVE difficulty getting erections or simply want to spruce up your sex life, chances are you’ve heard about honey packs. The sachets of the sweet stuff are all over social media, promising enhanced sexual performance through stronger, long-lasting erections.

At first glance, you might find this a “natural” alternative for young guys who don’t want pills or painful-sounding ED procedures like shock wave therapy. After all, the packets do feature pictures of honey and bees swarming on honeycombs, and honey is usually one of the first ingredients—a food many dudes already drizzle in oatmeal and tea. What could go wrong?

MH did a deep dive last year into whether honey packs actually work. The TL;DR version is that despite the alluring promise of near-instant, rock-hard erections, you’re really taking a gamble on what you’re putting in your body. Natural ingredients like honey and ginseng provide a “trivial” performance-enhancing effect and multiple honey pack supplement companies have been flagged by the FDA for having hidden and unknown dosages of ingredients not included in the label, like tadalafil (the active ingredient in Cialis), sildenafil (the active ingredient in Viagra), and acetaminophen.

That’s why doctors have big safety concerns about honey packs, says Scott Miller, MD, a urologist and director of robotic surgery at Wellstar Health System. “If they can’t tell me what’s in them, then it’s an absolute no.” So if honey packs are out, what are some ways to help you get hard and stay hard? We turned to the experts, asking urologists what they do to prepare in lieu of popping a pack.

HONEY PACKS (AND even gas station dick pills) aren’t worth your time or money. But not all supplements need to be ruled out, says Philip Werthman, MD, a urologist and director of the Center for Male Reproductive Medicine and Vasectomy Reversal. For guys with mild ED or who just want to optimize their libido, he recommends L-arginine supplements.

L-arginine is an amino acid that supports blood flow through nitric oxide production. Nitric oxide allows blood vessels to open fully and allow more blood flow to come into the penis.

“The penis is a hemodynamic organ. It works on blood flow. There has to be stimulation and a relationship that is functional between the nerves and the blood vessels,” says Dr. Werthman. “Anything that helps nitric oxide stick around longer will cause more blood flow to come in and maybe give a better quality erection.”

If possible, he recommends choosing L-arginine supplements containing L-citrulline (a precursor to L-arginine) or pycnogenol. The latter is an antioxidant made from the bark of a tree and is a powerful antioxidant used often in the fertility world, says Dr. Werthman. In concert with L-arginine, the combo helps to boost erections.

There is one caveat. For the effects to really work, you need to take this supplement on a daily basis. A single scoop the night before a sexual encounter won’t make much of a difference.

“It’s the kind of thing you put into your supplement stack,” says Dr. Werthman. Beyond healthy erections, nitric oxide helps with increasing blood flow all over the body, potentially providing extra benefits to your brain, heart, and muscles if you’re working out.

Buyer Beware: Supplements are not FDA-regulated, and some can get sketchy. Consider getting a product tested and certified by a third-party testing facility to verify the supplement’s safety and quality.

OYSTERS AND CHAMPAGNE get a lot of hype as aphrodisiacs. But Dr. Werthman says the true value is eating foods high in L-arginine. Here are some examples:

Additionally, watermelon is one of the best foods to eat on the day you’re having sex because of its high citrulline content, says Dr. Werthman. So, while spontaneous sex is great, scheduling sex can help you fuel your body (and boner) accordingly.

As for what’s on the don’t eat list? Nothing, but both urologists say it’s best to avoid alcohol before sex. You might gain a little liquid courage, but the buzz kills erections. Alcohol slows down brain signals related to arousal and decreases the ability of blood vessels to trap blood in the penis.

CORTISOL, ALSO KNOWN as your body’s stress hormone, is one of the biggest killers of testosterone and erections. When your body is in fight-or-flight mode, Dr. Werthman says, the last thing it’s thinking about is having sex.

The trademarks of a stressful lifestyle—lack of sleep, long working hours, and a poor diet—can all create barriers to intimacy, says Dr. Miller. Setting aside time to take care of yourself physically will help with performing at your best.

For example, a meditation session or some light stretching can relieve some stress temporarily. You also might want to consider a quick workout. Now, Dr. Werthman warns that a single sweat session won’t do much for your penile health (over time, consistent exercise does support blood flow and cardiovascular health, helping you last longer). But in terms of mental health, the stress-relieving benefits of pushups or a quick jog can help you get amped for the main event. Plus, the endorphins in your body can shake off any pre-sex nerves and make you feel more confident in your body. One study involving over 128,000 people found all types of physical activity—walking, resistance training, Pilates, and yoga—effective in improving anxiety symptoms.

Granted, for some people, sex itself is the stress reliever. But if you tense up thinking about the actual act, Dr. Werthman advises taking it slow. Get out of your head and focus on increasing erotic arousal through kissing and other forms of foreplay, then seeing if you want to go further. “It’s about being comfortable with your partner,” he says. “You want a dynamic where if you get a fail-to-launch situation, they understand. Because it happens—not every encounter leads to a touchdown.”
