#4982. Erin and Sara Foster Reveal the Rule That Keeps Their Business—and Sisterhood—Working

The Nobody Wants This producers stop by the latest episode of The Huddle.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’ve binged all three seasons of the Netflix comedy Nobody Wants This, presided over a board meeting in your chicest Favorite Daughter blazer, or nodded along to a cringey dating anecdote while listening to The World’s First Podcast, you are no doubt familiar with the work of multi-hyphenate sisters Erin and Sara Foster.

Raised in Los Angeles (dad is famous record producer David Foster), the sisters first gained notoriety with their VH1 mockumentary series, Barely Famous, in 2015. Since then, they’ve gone on to launch several successful businesses, including their clothing line and a production company, Fatigue Sisters Productions. (They even recently served as guest sharks on ABC’s Shark Tank.)

With the season 3 premiere of Nobody Wants This (based on Erin’s own experience of dating and marrying a Jewish man and later converting to Judaism), the dynamic duo stopped by the Women’s Health podcast The Huddle to chat with editors Abby Cuffey and Jacqueline Andriakos about doing business together, setting boundaries, and raising kids.

Erin and Sara launched their clothing line, Favorite Daughter, in late 2020 to fill gaps in their own closets. But as the company has grown and evolved over time, they’ve learned to put their customers at the heart of everything they do. It’s also forced the sisters to staff up with people who are willing to share their true opinions, rather than simply being yes-men or yes-women.

“That's something that is really challenging when you have a talent-focused brand,” Erin says. “It's taken a very long time for us to convince the people who work for us to be honest with us. That’s how people become monsters—no one's telling them the truth.”

“I always say, too, this is a democracy,” Sara adds. “This only works if everyone feels heard. This only works if you're allowed to do the thing that you're hired to do.”

Having a valued third or even fourth opinion also comes in handy when the two can’t see eye-to-eye, which happened often when the brand first launched.

“We’re in a good place today, but we would have blow-up screaming fights in fittings for many years at Favorite Daughter,” Erin says. “It’s tricky for us, because we do not have differentiated, carved-out roles. We have the exact same role, so if we disagree, it's really challenging to find the happy medium.”

In 2021, the sisters’ working relationship expanded further when they launched their podcast The World's First Podcast with Erin & Sara Foster. While the duo aren’t shy about diving into personal topics—be it romantic relationships or raising children—they have set certain boundaries to ensure their friends and family don’t end up embarrassed or as headline fodder.

“I have an idea of where [my husband’s] boundaries are,” Erin says. “He's not really into me talking about exes or other relationships.”

Sara, on the other hand, learned the hard way where one of her daughter’s boundaries lie when she revealed her juvenile arthritis diagnosis—in the hopes of helping other parents—and it was picked up by multiple outlets.

“It never occurred to me that that could happen,” Sara says. “My daughter was like, ‘I do not appreciate that.’ I was like, ‘Oh god, I'm so sorry.’”

Given that they have creative control over the podcast’s content, Erin and Sara do occasionally edit out portions that they think could be taken out of context with the TikTok-ification of media nowadays. “We try to err on the side of keeping things in, but then there's some times that you get a little ahead of yourself,” Erin says.

Speaking of raising daughters, Sara’s got even more wisdom to share on parenting—specifically about telling your kids the harsh truths about yourself.

“Being a mother is just such a exercise in getting humbled,” she says. “My instinct was always like, don't reveal yourself too much. Don't let them see your flaws. Don't tell them about all the times you f---ed up as a teenager yourself. But that's the opposite. You're really supposed to. Maybe some people disagree with this, but as they get older, you’re supposed to reveal mistakes you made, things that you wish you did differently... That has changed the dynamic with me and my older daughter—being honest with her about things that I wish I had done differently.”

Erin agrees: “I think it's probably better for your children to grow up knowing that you are a complicated, flawed person, and then you don't have to fall off a pedestal for them.”

To hear more from the sisters about how they find the creativity to create, their stance on kids and social media, and why they’re obsessed with a certain protein powder, click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above!

#4979. I’m Running the New York City Marathon Topless. The Reason Is Not What You Think.

It was my 18-mile long run, the farthest I'd gone so far in my New York City Marathon training, when I felt anxiety creep into my ankles. Central Park was full of life and happiness, but I was suddenly acutely aware of every mile, every ache, and every vulnerability I couldn't outrun. “I could just stop right now,” I thought.

A year earlier, I was in active treatment for breast cancer at 32. I had undergone chemotherapy, a mastectomy, and reconstruction, and was still learning to recognize my new body. Now, I was preparing to run 26.2 miles, completely topless, with my scars visible.

But I pushed through the fear: This was exactly why I chose to run in the first place. Not because I’ve overcome everything or that I have nothing left to hide—but because I’m learning to show up as I am: Uncomfortable, imperfect, and still moving forward. I’m running like this in the hopes that my story might help save another woman’s life. If seeing me and learning about my journey helps her speak up or look into her own breast cancer risk, this run becomes bigger than me.

In 2023, I left my career as an associate in wealth management at Merrill Lynch to raise my son. Six short months after I resigned, everything changed.

I found a lump. My ob-gyn told me I was too young for a mammogram. An ultrasound came back benign. It was a third doctor, a breast surgeon, who finally took me seriously and sent me for a mammogram, a biopsy, and an MRI. She saved my life.

I was leaving the gym on an ordinary Thursday when the call came. I had breast cancer in both breasts: stage 2 triple-negative cancer on one side and stage 1 ER/PR-positive cancer on the other.

The world went blurry, and every sound was muffled. Was I dying? My son was only one. I couldn't leave him without a mother, and my husband without his partner. I had so much more life to live, and so much more to do. How had the first two appointments missed this?

My husband, Elio, and I built my care team at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, and together we mapped out a plan: chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and surgeries. Each decision I made along the way helped me feel a little more in control.

One of the hardest parts of treatment was confronting how much my body had changed. When I finally had my mastectomy, I braced myself to be horrified when the bandages came off. I shed one tear. It hit me that things would never be the same and that a part of my body I'd tied to my femininity and sexuality had been changed forever. I faced a choice no woman should have to make. For me, it was this or facing my mortality.

But the moment that still gets me isn't the one in front of the mirror. It was the afternoon my then-two-year-old son caught a glimpse of my chest.

"Mommy, you have a boo boo?” He asked. “Are you hurt? Do you need to go to the hosminal?"

I had tried to protect my son from knowing what I was going through—no two-year-old should have to learn what cancer is before they learn the alphabet. But still, he could tell something was wrong. I was proud of his sympathy and awareness, but at the same time, I was heartbroken he noticed. I dreaded telling him about my cancer diagnosis—especially given my BRCA diagnosis and the unknowns about whether I had passed it along to him.

Later, changing in a gym locker room for the first time since surgery, I flinched, covering my chest as I pulled off my sports bra. I never would have done that before cancer. Was I ashamed of the scars? Nervous that I looked different? Probably a bit of both. I gave myself grace for that instinctive reaction, but also promised myself then that I would no longer let shame drive how I felt about my body. My scars are evidence that I lived. They stand for tenacity, resilience, and bravery—traits I want my son to have and how I want him to remember me.

During treatment, I set a goal to run my first half marathon a few months after my mastectomy. It kept me focused and gave me something to look forward to, something beyond appointments, medications, and the uncertainty of treatment. Crossing the finish line felt powerful. I thought of all the work that I’d put in to get there and the many training sessions where I chose to show up for myself every day.

But shortly after, I was disappointed to learn I would need to continue oral chemotherapy to help reduce the risk of recurrence. This pushed my recovery timeline back and meant I’d have to wait longer for my reconstructive surgeries. So I set another goal: if I could run 13.1 miles, I could run 26.2 the following year, when I’d be done with treatment and surgeries.

I decided I would also run topless, putting on display the very thing I vowed to never hide. No shirt, no bra. To prevent chafing and provide makeshift support, I plan on using special styling tape donated by NOOD.

I would do it for the women who might have questions they want to ask their doctors, who feel like something isn’t right but keep minimizing their concerns. And I would also do it for the other survivors out there. I hope that by seeing me run, they also feel more comfortable in their bodies, scars and all.

I set my sights on the New York City Marathon, running with Fred’s Team, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center’s charity partner. I even created a subteam, Team Laklak, named after the beauty brand I co-founded during my cancer journey, offering science-based makeup that’s still full of color and fun. I’m proud that we’ve raised $45,000 to date for the very hospital that saved my life. It feels like such a full-circle moment that the beauty company I dreamed up while sitting in treatment chairs there can now give back to other women in this way.

I’m not the first woman to run a marathon topless, but I will be the first in New York City. In 2024, Louise Butcher also ran the London Marathon, showing off the scars from her mastectomy and flat closure reconstruction for similar reasons. I chose to reconstruct with implants—and I’m not sure if people will find my run more taboo or sexualized because of it. They shouldn’t. Louise and I faced the same disease and underwent similar treatments.

On November 1, I'll finish my 26.2 miles back in Central Park, the same park where I once thought, “I could just stop right now.”

My story is about more than learning to embrace my body after cancer. It's also about what can happen when women are dismissed, when they question their instincts, or when they assume they are too young to be at risk.

Breast cancer doesn't discriminate by age. Approximately one in eight women in the United States will be diagnosed in their lifetime, and a diagnosis can happen well before the age many women associate with routine screening. I was fortunate to find a breast surgeon who listened to me and pursued further testing, but not every woman knows what questions to ask or where to turn when something doesn't feel right. A breast cancer risk assessment tool can be a useful place to start. While it cannot diagnose cancer or replace medical advice from a physician, it can help women better understand their personal risk and discuss whether additional evaluation or screening may be appropriate.

Whether we're navigating cancer or chasing a marathon finish line, we will all have moments when we want to stop. We may not feel fearless or ready. We may not know exactly what comes next. But we can take the next step, ask the next question, and learn to trust ourselves along the way.

I'm running topless because I no longer want to hide my scars. I'm running because I'm still here and because I can. But most of all, I'm doing this in the hope that another woman will feel a little more empowered to take charge of her own story.

Lauren Spiezia is a breast cancer survivor who carries the BRCA2 mutation and the founder of Laklak Beauty, a clean cosmetic brand built from her experience as an oncology patient. More at laklakbeauty.com/run.

#4978. The Men's Health Ultimate Guide to Peptides

A science-backed guide to understanding the use, side effects, and supporting research behind the emerging substances.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AS THE CURIOSITY around peptides grows, the FDA has made efforts in removing a portion of the 19 synthetic peptides from the Category 2 Bulk Substances List. This is kind of a huge deal because when the FDA classifies a substance as Category 2 they believe that it carries significant safety risks, and prohibit compounding pharmacies from making it.

In July 2026, an FDA advisory committee met to evaluate evidence for seven popular synthetic peptides on the Category 2 list and recommend whether the FDA should move them onto the Category 1 list, which allows them to be made. Another five will be under review in 2027.The FDA is not bound to the advisory committee’s recommendations.

The panel voted to loosen the restrictions on BPC-157 and TB-500 (those make up the infamous “Wolverine Stack”), as well as KPV, MOTS-C, Epitalon and Semax. It voted no for Emedeltide; that’s the one people reach for to help their sleep. None of the compounds scored a unanimous vote. This October, US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. pushed forward a policy to temporarily increase access to these six unapproved peptides. The government will not penalize licensed pharmacists in compounding pharmacies for creating and distributing these substances for people with a prescription. The nudge from RFK Jr. to allow the temporary sale of peptides has received mixed reactions.

”The American Peptide Association applauds the efforts of the Trump Administration and HHS to green light certain peptides into production by compound pharmacies,” Jeff Cohen, cofounder of the American Peptide Association wrote in an email to MH. “It is much needed clarity that the peptide industry, clinicians and consumers have hoped and worked for for the past couple years and is a bold step outside the usual pharma driven, FDA managed pathway.”

Motisola Lewis, MD, is an internal medicine physician who runs her own concierge medical practice working to fix a broken medical system. While she focuses on providing personalized care to her patients, she doesn’t agree with expanding access to unapproved peptides before having adequate evidence of their safety and effectiveness. “I want patients to have access to promising treatments, but I also want those treatments to be supported by good science. My concern is that the enthusiasm around peptides has moved much faster than the clinical evidence.” For Dr. Lewis, several questions are still missing that the FDA has not answered: do these peptides actually work and for whom, peptide quality especially from third-party suppliers, and who is in charge of oversight. That doesn’t mean she is unwilling to discuss peptides, which is happening more than ever.

Sritha Rajupet, MD, MPH, chair of the department of family, population, and preventive medicine at Stony Brook Medicine, also has concerns. “Most of these peptides still lack high-quality human data on safety, effectiveness, and appropriate dosing,” Dr. Rajupet says. Meaning that even if the FDA removes the Category 2 label, there’s still not a lot of research around if and how they work—along with any side effects. In the document outlining RFK Jr’s new policy, compounding pharmacists must report “serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded.”

Still, Dr. Rajupet acknowledges that people are interested in synthetic peptides—and many are already obtaining them through unregulated channels.

Kent Bradley, MD, sees this at his role of chief medical officer at 10X Health, which offers synthetic peptide therapy. “Many of the people reaching for peptides have already exhausted conventional options,” he says. “The issue we are seeing is that individuals may have gotten a peptide without going through legitimate quality checks of a compounded pharmacy and self-administering based on information they are seeing off of social media.”

The world of synthetic peptides is promising, for sure. But there are dangers—some of which are serious (ahem, cancer). Dr. Rajupet says that in order for consumers to protect themselves, they have to study up.

“From a clinical perspective, the priority is balancing harm reduction with scientific rigor—engaging patients in open, nonjudgmental conversations while being clear that many of these therapies remain experimental, with uncertain risks and benefits,” says Dr. Rajupet.

For this reason, we created a one-stop glossary to help answer your questions about the current peptide-palooza we’re in now. Here’s the hype—and actual science.

WELL, KNOW THAT peptides exist naturally. Technically, they’re short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of protein. And not just the kind of protein that builds biceps. Proteins can also act as messengers throughout your body, doing everything from signaling the release a particular hormone to regulating inflammatory responses.

But when we’re talking about the kind of peptides the FDA will consider for deregulation, we’re talking about synthetic peptides delivered through sprays or injection. These drugs work to trigger the same responses as natural peptides, but the science is in its very early stages. Anecdotal evidence from who take peptides have reported improvements in their health, appearance, and muscle performance. But, again, anecdotal.

These are the synthetic peptides that the FDA will consider for deregulation in 2026 and 2027, broken into categories based on their supposed health benefits. And we gave each a thumbs up, thumbs down, or thumbs "meh" to rate just how much the science backs up the supposed benefits.

Known as the fat burning peptide, AOD-9604 mimics human growth hormone to promote lipolysis, or the breakdown of stored fat. Scientists are using the peptide as a possible treatment for obesity and people are taking the peptide recreationally to burn body fat, boost fat metabolism, and support body recomposition. There is also discussion of AOD-9604 helping with joint pain, mobility, and collagen production. One of the supposed benefits of AOD-9604 is that it sheds fat without affecting blood sugar or inducing insulin resistance.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: The studies on the effectiveness and safety of AOD-9604 go back roughly a decade. The research was largely conducted on animals and most of the studies that showed positive results were funded or led by researchers from the pharmaceutical company that developed AOD-9604.

This peptide reportedly protects the cell by providing more “fuel” for increased stamina. So people who report fatigue are taking the peptide to improve energy and metabolism. Because MOTS-C is supposed to target mitochondria, the energy sources of a cell, you’ll see it promoted in longevity stacks.RESEARCH SUMMARY: While there has been extensive research into the physiological function of MOTS-C, there is a lack of clinical trial data testing the safety and effectiveness of the peptide.

Semax is considered a brain-boosting peptide often given as a nasal spray. Anecdotal reports detail improvements in memory, attention, and deeper mental awareness. Semax is supposed to work by raising a protein called brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) that is important for learning and strengthening connection between brain cells.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Most of the research in Semax that claims it has neuroprotective effects come from Russia, where the peptide is used in the treatment of people with stroke. The Alzheimer’s Drug Discovery Foundation reviewed the Russian pilot studies in humans and found a lack of strong evidence demonstrating that Semax would improve cognition in healthy individuals or in the prevention of cognitive aging. (Although a recent 2025 study from Russia found evidence of Semax injections reducing amyloid plaques in rat models of Alzheimer’s). Older studies using rats found improved cognition 15 minutes after injection, likely by stimulating BDNF production. There is a lack of safety data, especially in long-term side effects, in humans. One review reported discoloration of the nasal cavity and increased blood sugar levels in people with diabetes. Not great.

Selank is a nootropic touted for reducing anxiety and stress while increasing cognitive performance. Anecdotal evidence calls Selank a “life-changer” for anxiety and sleep, with some people feeling relaxed but not drowsy, as well as more focused.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Selank’s anxiolytic and cognitive protective effect along with relieving stress have only been studied in rodents and molecular studies. Older mice studies have also found evidence of improved learning and memory performance after a single injection of Selank.

TB-500 is a peptide intended for muscle recovery, increased flexibility, and joint stability. Users often pair the synthetic peptide with BPC-157 to further boost muscle recovery. TB-500 works by binding to a structural protein in cells called actin. By up-regulating actin, TB-500 purportedly speeds cell movement for tissue repair.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There is a good amount of animal research on Thymosin Beta-4 and its accelerated healing effects on skin and muscle fibers. While there is a body of preclinical research on the peptide, there’s a lack of studies looking at the synthetic peptide TB-500. Plus, there is no clinical evidence in humans that Thymosin Beta-4 or TB-500 repairs muscles or increases athletic performance.

More concerning are studies linking elevated Thymosin Beta-4 levels with the development of cancer. Through the same mechanisms that promote wound healing, Thymosin Beta-4 may enhance tumor angiogenesis, the process where cancer cells stimulate new blood vessels, which provides them oxygen and nutrients to grow and spread.

Known as the “Wolverine” or “Body Protection Compound,” the synthetic peptide reportedly helps with tissue repair and anti-inflammatory effects. Users champion the peptide’s ability to speed recovery from intensive workouts or even injury. BPC-157 does not directly build muscle mass.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Animal data on BPC-157 showed evidence of the peptide helping with musculoskeletal injuries. However, there is little data showing the effects in humans.

The natural form of this peptide helps with increasing and restoring immune function. It works by enhancing antibody response and T-cell activity. People taking the synthetic, injectable form report immediate improvement in their well-being after long COVID and other immune disorders. Outside of the US, Thymosin Alpha-1 is approved in over 30 countries for treating hepatitis and other infections.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Five large clinical trials on the peptide have found Thymosin Alpha-1 reduces inflammation and infection in people with severe acute pancreatitis. That’s likely due to the peptide’s ability to rebalance immune cell distribution, including boosting the percentages of CD4+ T cells. Thymosin Alpha-1 has also been shown to enhance vaccine response and help people with severe COVID by repairing damage caused by inflammation. However, one large phase 3 clinical trial in people with sepsis found an injection of thymosin alpha 1 did not improve mortality outcomes.

People taking the synthetic form of this peptide report doing so to reduce inflammation and improve skin health. (Some say it can clear up eczema, psoriasis, and acne.) There are also some people with inflammatory bowel conditions, such as Crohn’s and IBD, who say that KPV has helped their gut health. The peptide reportedly works by inhibiting several pro-inflammatory pathways while preserving other immune responses.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There’s not sufficient data on KPV to conclusively say it helps in humans. The most cited research on KPV is a 2008 study, which found that the peptide reduced intestinal inflammation in human intestinal cells. Yes, that was many, many years ago.

This neuropeptide reportedly promotes falling asleep faster, as well as increasing how much time you spend in restorative deep, slow-wave sleep. in Stage 3 sleep. Anecdotal evidence of people taking the synthetic form of this peptide states that in helps with staying asleep, increasing sleep duration, and entering deep sleep.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: DSIP research on humans is extremely limited. Most research looking into DSIP’s role in sleep took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed results. While a small clinical trial did report sleep-promoting effects, other studies found it ineffective or from a placebo effect. Research in the 2000s has been focused on animals and how DSIP could help protect against cancer or improve motor ability after stroke.

This peptide has links to sexual function. It works by stimulating the release of the hormone, gonadotropin, which results in an increase of testosterone. People who take synthetic kisspeptin-10 have reported a greater libido, ability to maintain an erection, and enjoy orgasm, along with reduced anxiety—especially surrounding sexual response.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: There is animal and human research that shows kisspeptin-10 stimulates gonadotrophin release. Most notably, a small clinical trial found that men with low sexual desire experienced increases in “penile tumescence” (their term, not ours), as well as greater attraction and arousal. There were no side effects reported.

Epitalon is the natural form of the peptide, and it’s been used to treat chronic insomnia, especially in people who don’t respond to sleep medications. By raising melatonin, the peptide would allegedly regulate circadian rhythms and promote better sleep. Epithalamin is the synthetic peptide and people are reportedly taking it for anti-aging effects, both cognitive and aesthetic.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Epitalon has not been tested in people for slowing or preventing cognitive decline. Most of the early preclinical and clinical studies on epitalon’s effects on anti-aging, cognition, and sleep come from Russia and mainly from the lab of the now-deceased Dr. Vladimir Kh. Khavinson. The few studies in human cells (note, not actual humans) suggest that epitalon extends telomere length. Telomeres are the protective caps at the end of chromosomes to protect from damage. In terms of safety, there is a lack of data, especially on its short-term and long-term toxicity effects.

The natural GHK-Cu peptide is used for promoting skin health. People using the synthetic drug are using GHK-Cu to stimulate collagen and elastin production to tighten aging skin, reduce wrinkles, fade scars, and repair the skin barrier. People have anecdotally reported thicker, fuller hair after using the peptide as it supposedly reduces inflammation and increases blood circulation to the scalp.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Topical GHK-Cu is commonly used in cosmetics to increase collagen production, promote wound healing, and improve skin health. It has a good safety profile because it has limited low-level skin absorption. Injectable and oral versions of GHK-Cu may come with several potentially life-threatening risks.

This peptide is a selective agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR1) that stimulates the pituitary gland to release growth hormone production. (Yeah, it’s complex.) Just know that people are excited about Ipamorelin because the peptide reportedly increases muscle mass and strength.

Online forums dedicated to Ipamorelin mention that taking the peptide does not increase appetite, cortisol, or prolactin like other growth hormone peptides. In addition to strength improvements, other ancedotes discuss skin and hair benefits. Ipamorelin is typically paired with other peptides, such as CJC-1295.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: Animal studies have shown that Ipamorelin is effective in stimulating the pituitary gland to release growth hormones. However, there is a lack of large clinical trials that show the peptide works in humans.

This peptide binds to receptors in the pituitary gland to stimulate the secretion of growth hormone and production of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). People are taking CJC-1295 to build muscle, reduce recovery time, and increase fat metabolism. A common stack among the longevity community is CJC-1295 and Ipamorelin for its synergistic effects to maintain lean muscle, get better sleep, and reduce fatigue.

RESEARCH SUMMARY: While clinical data has shown promising results of CJC-1295 to increase growth hormone production, the peptide is linked to a number of adverse events.

The following five peptides are likely to stay on the Category 2 list because of a lack of clinical evidence and/or significant safety concerns.

SIDE EFFECTS: Infection, potential death, fluctuating blood sugar levels, pancreatitis

SIDE EFFECTS: Increase appetite, possible changes in cortisol levels, and increases in blood sugar levels

USE: “Sunless” tanning and to stimulate erections in men with erectile dysfunction

SIDE EFFECTS: Severe adverse events including melanoma, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, sympathomimetic toxidrome, and priapism

USE: Increasing immune defenses and fight against infections

SIDE EFFECTS: Nonclinical research has found adverse effects on the male reproduction system and potentially cancer development

SIDE EFFECTS: Insufficient information on whether it’s safe for humans

#4976. How to Lose Fat and Build Muscle Sustainably as a Busy Mom—Your Realistic 4-Step Plan

A strength coach for moms outlines the key strength training and diet habits to adopt for lasting change.

For many moms returning to exercise after pregnancy, losing fat while building muscle can feel like a daunting goal.

“The odds are good that you lost some muscle mass during pregnancy. Maybe you weren’t training as much as you normally did or you weren’t training at all,” says Bailey, coach and founder of Well Mamas Coaching, in a recent YouTube video.

However, body recomposition is a gradual process, she explains, and consistency—“sticking with it”—matters far more than getting everything right.

“It's not [about] doing it perfectly. It's not having an hour to yourself every single day to do all this magical meal prep and green juicing,” she says.

“It's just jumping back in when you can and not buying into the start-stop cycle of...start[ing] over on Monday and find[ing] a new plan.”

Strength training with progressive overload is a “gold standard” pillar of a realistic body recomposition plan, Bailey says.

Progressive overload means gradually making your workouts more challenging over time by increasing the weight, number of repetitions, or training frequency, or by reducing your rest periods.

“This type of strength training is what signals your body...to adapt, change, and rebuild the muscle fibers that we're tearing down during these workouts, which is what helps you build muscle,” Bailey explains.

She recommends focusing on compound exercises such as squats, lunges, deadlifts, hip thrusts, and the bench press because “you're recruiting multiple muscle groups.”

As for your workout schedule, she reassures viewers that you don't need to train “six times a week...for 45 to 60 minutes.”

“Four workouts a week, 30 minutes or less, with progressive overload and compound moves...is plenty,” she says.

By now, it's well established that muscle growth and repair depend on eating enough protein.

“If you're not eating enough protein to repair the tears that you create in your muscles when you work out, then your body doesn't have the amino acids it needs to build those muscle fibers,” Bailey says.

She recommends aiming for around 30g of protein per meal. That's broadly in line with research showing that consuming around 25-30g of protein per meal is associated with greater lean mass and both upper- and lower-body strength in healthy women.

Good options include lean meat, beans, and legumes, yogurt, cottage cheese, and canned tuna.

“Mild” is the key word, Bailey emphasizes.

A calorie deficit means consuming fewer calories than your body burns each day.

“Of course, you do need to be in some sort of caloric deficit in order for fat loss to occur,” she reminds viewers.

However, the size of that deficit matters.

She recommends a moderate deficit of around 200-400 calories below your maintenance intake.

“That's just enough to prompt your body to use stored fat for energy,” she explains. “However, it's not so much that your body starts cannibalizing muscle.”

Research supports the importance of avoiding an overly aggressive calorie deficit, with one study finding that eating more than 500 fewer calories than required impaired gains in lean mass.

She adds one caveat for breastfeeding moms.

“You want to go above what I would calculate if you weren't nursing—anywhere from 400-800 additional calories per day,” she says.

Bailey acknowledges this can be difficult for moms.

“Often sleep and stress feel like they're not within our control,” she says.

However, sleep is essential because it's during recovery that muscle adapts and grows.

“The muscle...broken down through resistance training...is rebuilt...during sleep, while we're recovering,” she explains.

She also references research showing that sleep duration influences body recomposition, with shorter sleep associated with less fat loss.

If “a solid eight hours” isn't realistic, she suggests finding even a few extra minutes by cutting back on doomscrolling or late-night TV.

She also notes that chronically elevated cortisol levels associated with stress may interfere with muscle-building processes, recommending outdoor walks, deep breathing, or even guided meditation in the shower to create small moments of calm.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

But also, it’s not totally your fault. But foreplay is important because it prepares people mentally, emotionally, and physically for the main sexual experience, he explains. On a physical level, foreplay usually causes increased blood flow to the penis, resulting in an erection. It also increases blood flow to the vagina, and especially the clitoris, increasing pleasure, lubrication, and sensitivity. Meanwhile, on a mental level, foreplay gets the brain all excited, releasing feel-good chemicals such as dopamine and oxytocin. And, on the all-important emotional level, it allows you and your partner to build up a sense of connection and intimacy, says Spann.

Essentially, you should think of foreplay as less of a “before” activity, and more of an integral addition to mind-blowing hookups, no matter the type of sex you’re having.

After all, for many women and people with vulvas, foreplay is actually the main event. Only 18 percent of women can orgasm from intercourse alone, per a 2018 study. For nearly 37 percent of women, clitoral stimulation is necessary to climax during sex, and another 36 percent say that, while clit stimulation might not be necessary, their orgasms feel better when it’s part of the process.

In fact, they’re part of what’s called the “golden quartet of orgasm,” a.k.a. four sexual behaviors that are the strongest predictors of women’s orgasms. The biggest predictor was manual stimulation of genitals, a.k.a. fingering, followed by using a sex toy, then receiving oral sex, and finally, deep kissing.

Here’s the thing about being “good in bed”—it’s about so much more than what you do in bed. “Foreplay starts the minute your last sexual encounter ends,” says Nicolle Dirksen, LPC, a sex and couples therapist in Minneapolis, Minnesota. “This means we have to shift the way we think about foreplay. It’s not just some kissing and touching in bed for the few minutes leading up to penetration. It’s all of the flirting, stolen kisses, and booty pats in between.”

Fun fact: You don’t even have to be in the same room to start foreplay. Sending a little text like “Can’t wait to get naked with you tonight” builds anticipation, says Spann, which, consequently, builds arousal. (And if sending nudes turns you and your partner on, go ahead and swap sexy pics.)

But before you get all hot and heavy...

Your space doesn’t have to be spotless, but get rid of anything obviously gross. Put dirty clothes in the hamper (and the hamper in your closet), wash your dishes, and throw away any trash.

Granted, this may not always be possible in the heat of the moment. “Sometimes, sex is sporadic, and we don't have time for all of that,” Spann says. “But if you’re able to prepare for someone to come over, make sure the environment is welcome.” Pro tip: If you’re going out with the hopes of bringing someone back to yours, spend 10 minutes sprucing up your place before you leave. No matter how you end your night, at least you’ll be coming home to a clean room.

As you’re tidying up, nix any additional distractions that might take away from the sexual experience. “When we’re distracted, our brake system gets activated, which shuts off our ability to get turned on,” says Wright. “When we remove distractions as best we can, we eliminate factors that could stop us from getting turned on, which is the primary point of foreplay.”

So please, silence your notifications, turn off the TV, and put away any work so the mood isn’t broken by the ping of a text or a commercial about antifungal cream.

Selecting the right music can make or break just about any situation, and foreplay is no exception. In general, though, throwing on some tunes can help drown out distractions (most of which you eliminated above, right?) and keep the momentum going. Plus, music can help your space feel welcoming and create a relaxing vibe, says Spann.

A casual question like “You okay if I play some music?” is a clear but simple way to show you care about your partner feeling comfortable in your space, says Spann. (Btw, you can also suggest playing music if that will help you feel comfortable in their space.)

“Slow it down, slow it down,” says Spann. “You might be horny and desiring penetration, but [one of the main] benefits of foreplay is that you actually get to take your time.” This can be particularly helpful for men who tend to ejaculate prematurely, he adds, since devoting more time to foreplay can help you extend the sexual experience.

You might think all you want to do is rip each other’s clothes off and get to thrusting, but try taking off one article of clothing at a time and exploring each other’s bodies as they’re revealed to you. “That allows you to enjoy touch and be connected to the person that you're with,” says Spann.

Sure, there’s a certain value to a quickie when you’re truly strapped for time—but in any other scenario, it’s best to heed the old adage: Slow and steady wins the race.

When in doubt, just come right out and ask what your partner likes during foreplay. “Most [people] appreciate men who want to make sure they’re satisfied,” says Barbara Bartlik, MD, a professor of psychiatry at Cornell University. Communication is essential for good sex, no matter what kind of sex you’re having. Being open and honest about your turn-ons and inviting your partner to do the same creates an erotic atmosphere that’s both sexy and trusting.

“Women get their greatest erotic pleasure from frequent, passionate kissing,” says Patti Britton, PhD, clinical sexologist, and author of The Art of Sex Coaching: Expanding Your Practice. “If you get the sense that she’s starting to lose interest, kissing is always the best way to bring her back into it.” That said, kissing is enjoyable for everyone, regardless of gender, so why not keep up puckering up?

Just remember that passionate kissing doesn’t always mean frantically swabbing your partner's tonsils. Try to mix up your tongue play with the occasional closed-mouth kiss on their nose, eyes, and forehead.

Remember how thrilling dry humping was before the days of penetration? It’s actually just as hot—if not more so—as an adult, so consider adding it into your foreplay repertoire. “If dry humping is an accelerator for you (meaning it turns on your sexual activation system), dry hump away,” Wright says. “We want to give the body time to adjust to a space of activation and pleasure, so anything that turns on your sexual system and makes the blood flow to your genitals is good foreplay.”

#4973. Overhead wired charging comes to Austin electric bus fleet

CapMetro’s Austin transit fleets electrified two public bus lines and opened two new park-and-ride facilities featuring overhead pantograph-style wired charging equipment to help Austinites breathe a little bit easier.

Originally announced in June, CapMetro’s two new park-and-ride stations are now open. Dubbed the Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center facilities debuted alongside the agency’s Rapid 800 and 837 electric bus routes, adding upgraded passenger amenities and end-of-line charging infrastructure to support its growing fleet of electric transit buses.

At CapMetro’s main bus depot, infrastructure partner Camber Charging supplied and installed two 1,440 kW charging systems connected to 48 industrial dispensers. The installation provides 2.9 MW of total charging capacity, and is designed to support overnight charging for up to 48 electric buses simultaneously.

The new Goodnight Ranch and Expo Center terminals extend that infrastructure along the Rapid 800 and 837 routes with the overhead pantograph chargers that are the big news here, allowing buses to top off their batteries at the end of each line and eliminate any lingering range anxiety for the trip back.

“Instead of a typical bus holding 8 hours of charging, on-route charging takes that out to 20 to 22 hours,” explains CapMetro Chief Operations Officer and Executive VP, Andy Skabowski. “Every time that pantograph drops, we charge that bus. That’s what makes a commitment like (every) 10- to 15-minute service possible.”

The buses themselves are built on Canadian manufacturer New Flyer’s Xcelsior battery-electric transit platform (battery specs aren’t included in the release, but New Flyer claims up to 660 kWh of available capacity). And, with up to 320 all-electric hp with all its torque available at 0 rpm, the city’s 48 electric buses will have no problem navigating Austin’s stop-and-go traffic.

This seems like a logical cost effective solution. In theory, this should enable transit systems to purchase busses with smaller batteries which would surely offset the cost of the new charging infrastructure.

Camber Charging provides preventive maintenance, charger and energy management software and remote diagnostics across all three locations.

SOURCE | IMAGES: CapMetro, via Charged EVs.

#4972. 5 Reasons to Fall in Love with La Quinta

Whether you’re visiting to play, explore, or simply chill, this desert paradise in California’s Coachella Valley has a little something for everyone.

Every day, from deciding whether or not to hit snooze to choosing to read a few more pages before shutting our eyes, our brains are a blur of choices—approximately 35,000 according to prevailing research. And frankly, it’s exhausting trying to make the right one every time. A vacation reboot would help… but travel planning requires even more decisions, which obviously defeats the purpose. And so the trip gets backburnered again.

What if there was a place that made choosing easy—because there’s no possible wrong answer? A land where you could decide to do all the things on the visitor’s bureau checklist, or none of them, and have an equally good time?

Enter La Quinta, California, a city of championship golf courses, towering palms, sprawling resorts with pools and spas, Old Hollywood lore, dramatic mountain backdrops, purple skies at dusk, and savory restaurants tucked into a calm corner of the Coachella Valley. It’s a place where you’re encouraged to do only what you love and what makes you feel most alive. Here in this sun-kissed slice of paradise, choose to follow the itinerary that is most Quinta-ssentially you.

There are 20 golf courses within the city limits, including the nine at the PGA West, a 2,000-acre luxury golf resort and community. Among those are the Mountain Course and the Stadium Course, which blend stunning natural beauty, manicured landscapes, challenging holes and expert designs by masters Pete Dye, Jack Nicklaus, and Greg Norman.

You can hit up the pickleball and tennis courts at Fritz Burns Park from dawn until well past dusk. The 12-acre green space also features a skate park, a children’s playground, a pool, and a dedicated area to play fetch with your pup. If you need to brush up on the rules of your chosen game, book some time with the pros at La Quinta Resort & Club, where you can rent equipment or pick up a match.

Whether you’re craving laid-back brunch bites, like the huckleberry hotcakes or double smashburgers at the farm-to-table eatery Beautiful Day, or a night on the town enjoying minty lamb chops and mai tais exploding with citrusy pucker at DSRT Club, La Quinta’s culinary scene does not disappoint.

Greet the day with Mexican delicacies like machaca or chilaquiles on the colorful porch at Casa Mendoza. If you have a hankering for south-of-the-border specialties later in the day, they also make a mean molcajete, seafood enchiladas, or tacos al pastor. Come afternoon, head to La Quinta Cliffhouse for the legendary nightly happy hour and stay for supper at sunset. There, you can put the date in date night by snacking on Medjools with bacon, blue cheese, coconut, and honey. (Pro tip: always order the gooey stone fruit however it’s served, whether as a shake, syrup or side dish—the Coachella Valley grows 95% of the dates in the U.S.) Close out the night with a slice of decadent Toll House Pie, a fixture at The Sandbar for four decades.

Those who believe it is just as important to nourish the mind as it is the body can take a walk down memory lane at the free La Quinta Museum, where the newly expanded history and culture exhibit details the people, technologies, and businesses that shaped the city, including the Cahuilla Indians, homesteaders, the railroad, and the celebrity magnet La Quinta Resort, which is celebrating its centennial this year. At the museum, visual learners can study the massive mural and a collection of photographs.

La Quinta itself is a patron of the arts. It’s hard to miss the more than 160 sculptures, murals, and decorated utility boxes installed through the Art In Public Places program. Twice a year, creatives from around the world descend on the civic center campus and turn it into a concert venue and an alfresco art gallery for a four-day festival. After admiring the artwork, head over to Old Town for locally made mementos. The charming retail district—known for its pleasing Spanish colonial architecture and vibrant sprays of bougainvillea—stocks gems at independent boutiques and galleries year-round and hosts the open-air Art on Main Street event on select Saturdays from November to April.

The area is a bonanza for outdoor activity. Bike along the base of the Santa Rosa Mountains using the paved, 2.7-mile-long Bear Creek Trail, or fix your attitude by gaining altitude on the miles of trails littered throughout the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto mountain ranges.

One popular route takes hikers a little more than six miles from the La Quinta Cove neighborhood to Lake Cahuilla, which is particularly peaceful at dawn or dusk. (The luckiest trekkers spy bighorn sheep.) Go straight to the lake to picnic, go horseback riding, or fish. Prolong your city escape by pitching a tent and camping at Cahuilla. Sunrise yoga and movie screenings are also offered lakeside.

While it’s clear there’s lots to do, know that, in the LQ, doing nothing is always on the table. Downtime happens to be a desert specialty, as there’s always a cold pool, a chaise lounge, and an umbrella drink calling your name. In fact, La Quinta Resort & Club boasts 42 pools across the 45-acre property, including a family-friendly splash zone and a more serene adults-only plunge with private cabanas and movie nights. (Don’t forget the 53 hot tubs for crisp Coachella nights.) Those who enjoy night swimming should post up at the never-closed pool at The Chateau at Lake La Quinta.

Finish the evening with stargazing and a glass of something sparkling in front of the fire pits. To really lean into relaxation, melt into a hot stone massage at Coral Spa or happily drift off while indulging in chromotherapy, a steam bath, or a dreamy scalp rub at Spa La Quinta. Or tap into an even deeper state of zen by joining a meditation or breathwork session or Sound Bath Sundays at Gather Yoga in Old Town. Plan your easiest trip ever today.

#4970. Yozma IN 11 review: The OG mini e-moto gets updates galore

…including 4.5kW motor, bigger 1.4kWh battery and 45mph top speed

Yozma may not have invented the mini moto space, but they certainly helped mainstream it. Together with Tuttios and Sur Rons, Yozma’s IN10 was one of the most popular mini motos out there, and if you surveyed the average group of 14-15-year-olds in a suburban rideout, you’d be hard-pressed not to find at least a few Yozma IN10s among them…

Today Yozma is shipping the IN 11 ($100 off with code 9TO5TOYS100), which attempts to bridge the gap between entry-level mini-bikes and high-end off-roaders, but at what cost?

Taken in a vacuum, the Yozma IN11 is an impressive update to the IN 10 and actually is more closely specced to the bigger IN10 Pro.

But we of course, don’t live in a vacuum, and others, including the Heybike Villain and the Engwe Eagle have already brought 52V, 4.5kW motors to the pit bike form factor, sometimes at much lower cost.

I should say here that parents who want to keep their kids’ e-motos in the 20-30mph range are going to be a whole lot happier with the 2.6kW than 4.5kW motors. Two nice safety improvements over the original Yozma IN10 include the magnetic kill switch and brake lights on the IN11.

If we are keeping it real here, there are dozens of similar-sized and spec’d mini-e-motos out there, often at a much lower cost than the Yozma IN11. But I’d argue that as the biggest and most trusted of these brands, Yozma is a safer bet.

Also, the IN11 is just a lot more solid than the random Amazon/Alibaba electric pit bike. Putting the IN11 together is quicker and easier than any other emoto I’ve built, and it just feels a lot more solid.

That feeling extends to the safety features. The brakes are more dialed in. The turning feels a lot tighter, and the overall ride is quieter and lighter. I believe, and my limited testing bears this out, that spec for spec, I got a lot more range on the IN11 than I got on other bikes with similar battery and motor specs. That 200nm of torque feels like it belongs on a much more expensive e-moto.

The smart wheelie mode is a nice trick (15, 25, or 40 degrees wheelie settings) and something we’ve only seen on Anylands for this price point so far. It is less of a standout feature on the IN11, and we expect to see this on just about every new pit bike coming out over the next few years. In fact, we’ve got another one in the review queue now.

That said, the price, which is currently fluctuating between $1299 and $1499 (don’t forget your $100 off 9TO5TOYS100 code), Yozma is going to be on the more expensive side of the 4.5kW emotos out there and some of the less established and more sketchy newcomers are bringing an intense value competition to the place where Yozma once dominated by itself.

#4968. Why Women Over 50 Should Add This Underrated Carry to Their Strength Routine

“Many people think core training means crunches or planks, but one of the most functional ways to strengthen the core is by learning to resist movement,” says personal trainer Alice Jordan.

Her go-to exercise for doing exactly that? The kettlebell suitcase carry.

“Holding a kettlebell in one hand and walking with good posture forces the deep abdominal muscles, obliques, and spinal stabilizers to work continuously to keep your body upright,” explains Jordan, who specializes in strength training during perimenopause.

“For women over 50, this is particularly valuable because it develops balance, posture and stability while also improving grip strength, which is an important marker of healthy aging,” notes Jordan.

Indeed, one landmark study published in The Lancet found that lower grip strength was consistently associated with a higher risk of early death—even after accounting for age, physical activity, smoking, body size, and other cardiovascular risk factors. Notably, the researchers reported that grip strength predicted somebody’s risk of dying better than systolic blood pressure.

The single-arm kettlebell suitcase carry, adds Jordan, “also translates directly into everyday activities such as carrying shopping, lifting luggage, or playing with grandchildren, making it a highly functional exercise.”

Below, Jordan explains how to do the exercise effectively and safely.

“Aim to include the exercise 2-3 times per week as part of a strength training program. It’s particularly effective when performed after your main strength exercises or as part of your core training,” adds Jordan.

As for how heavy a weight you should use for this exercise, Jordan recommends “choosing a kettlebell that feels challenging while still allowing you to maintain perfect posture throughout the walk.”

“You should be able to resist leaning to one side, keep your shoulders level and your core engaged from start to finish,” she adds.

“As a general guide, beginners might start with around 15-20 lb, while those with more strength training experience may use 20-30 lb or heavier, depending on their ability.”

Below, Jordan highlights four key mistakes to avoid while performing this exercise.

#4967. The Man Behind Fashion’s Most Dazzling Spectacles Turns His Attention to the Art of Light

For as long as he can remember, Alexandre de Betak has been entranced by light. As a 10-year-old, he rewired his Paris bedroom so that visitors had to be buzzed in, greeted by shifting colored lights. He went on to found Bureau Betak, a set design agency that transformed the runway with its megawatt spectacles for clients like Dior, Gucci, Jacquemus, and Fendi. De Betak estimates that he produced “thousands” of fashion shows—including Saint Laurent’s spring-summer 2020 ready-to-wear extravaganza, for which he bathed the Eiffel Tower in golden light, and installations for Rodarte featuring fluorescent and neon tubes.

A new truss light sculpture by Alexandre de Betak, seen here in a 17th-century Swedish castle

Now, de Betak, who sold his company in 2021, is turning the spotlight on his own creative practice. On November 5, he opened his first solo exhibition of artworks at Salon 94 in New York. The electronically programmed Truss Light Sculptures are inspired by the scaffolding and fixtures of his early runway shows and in some cases literally made from them. “That equipment is old-fashioned now, but I wanted to honor it,” de Betak says. “And I liked the irony that I spent so much energy over the years trying to hide it.”

On view at Salon 94’s Upper East Side town house through December 19, the exhibit presents two series. In the gallery’s contemporary space, the first is composed of freestanding and wall-mounted aluminum structures fitted with LED bulbs. The upstairs Stone Room, a historic space with Caen stone plaster walls and arched windows, is the backdrop for a second series of versions in bronze. To make them, de Betak had a French foundry recast each part down to the smallest screw by hand, a process that sometimes required more than 20 molds.

A pair of wall-mounted sculptures in aluminum

The light sculptures, which vary from sconce-like creations to hulking constructions out of a sci-fi movie, have a sly sense of humor and a human quality. This is especially true when they come to life, thanks to a remote-control-operated system that activates light sequences that glow, sparkle, thrum, or react to ambient noise, “whether a whisper,” de Betak says, “or extremely loud music.” For these effects, he drew on his stage work, where he was renowned for cueing, or choreographing, light and sound. “I’m interested in the ephemeral nature of what this equipment was made to show—whether a fashion show or a ballet,” he says. “At a moment when everything is virtual, I think it’s more important than ever to create things that produce a live emotion.”

Salon 94’s founder Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn observes that de Betak’s sculptures are equally powerful switched on or off. Unlit they remind her of David Smith artworks or Russian constructivism. Lit, and with synced sound, they evoke the theatricality of stage performers. “Alex has spent his career building structures that disappear into someone else’s spectacle,” she says. “Here, the structure is the whole point.”

#4964. The Men's Health 30-Day Workout Challenge

You can get moving to get in shape—but you have to commit.

SOMETIMES, THE MOST challenging part of working out is knowing what to do.

You might not have a definite goal in mind other than that you want to get moving, or that you want to look different by the time the summer season rolls around. That's okay. Not everyone is wired to constantly aspire to build muscle or run fast, following a detailed program designed to elicit peak performance and radical transformation. Just wanting to get active to live a healthier life is a worthy goal, especially if you're taking your first steps to make fitness part of your daily routine or recommitting to exercise after a break. But you have to be ready to commit to your new routine for it to be effective.

That's what the Men's Health 30-Day Workout Challenge is all about: doing something every day. Rather than limiting the focus to just one specific body part, muscle group, or type of exercise, as we have with our previous challenges, we're more interested in establishing healthy habits and introducing you to common exercise protocols that will be useful for the rest of your fitness life. Beginners can take the challenge and hold their own, while fitness pros can still push themselves to work to their full potential using these routines.

The plan is simple. You'll take on a new workout routine every day—but there will be some consistencies so you won't be constantly thrown into the deep end if you don't have a ton of experience. All of the workouts will be comprised out of a pool of just 11 exercises, which you can see demonstrated below by the program's architect, Men's Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S.

Each week of the program will be focused on a different workout scheme, so you can get the swing of the structure and get comfortable within each protocol. The calendar will also be structured in a manner that allows you to flex all of your muscles, both figuratively and literally; Day 1 of each week will be focused on Mobility and Core, Day 2 is Upper Push/Pull, Day 3 is Lower body, Day 4 is a Mobility focus, Day 5 is Upper Push/Pull, Day 6 is an Upper/Lower/Core split, and Day 7 is all Core.

All you have to do is buy in. By Day 30 (or the bonus Day 31, if you're game), at the very least you'll have completed this challenge. If you put in max effort, you'll also be moving better, feeling fitter, and looking different than you did on Day 1.

For each interval workout, work for 40 seconds, then take 20 seconds off unless otherwise stated. Repeat for 2 rounds. The goal: Work for quality reps for each move.

• Minute 1: Spiderman Lunge to T-Spine• Minute 2: Hollow Rock• Minute 3: Plank Shoulder Tap• Minute 4: Mountain Climber

• Minute 1: Glute Bridge Reach• Minute 2: Bent-Over T• Minute 3: Pushup• Minute 4: Bent-Over T

#4963. How to Organize a Kitchen Pantry in 6 Easy Steps, According to Experts

A pantry is among the most hardworking areas of the home, but without proper skills, it can also turn into the most cluttered. Learning how to organize a kitchen pantry like a pro requires a pro, so we tapped expert organizers to share their best pantry organization tips. Ahead, you’ll find a step-by-step guide to organizing your pantry—and keeping it that way. The process includes decluttering expired items, grouping pantry staples by category, deciding what to place on upper and lower shelves, and utilizing food storage containers and labeled bins. Whether you have a spacious walk-in pantry or you’re working with limited shelf space, use these pantry organization ideas to maximize vertical space, function, and style.

Start by removing everything from your pantry. “As you are taking the items out, take note of expiration dates and toss anything that is past its best by date, that is stale, or is no longer edible,” says Megan Barnhart, a professional organizer and founder of Barnhart Home. Since the pantry is rarely empty, take the opportunity to deep-clean it—wipe pull-out shelves, wash pantry storage vessels, and sweep the floor. You can also use this time to place liners or contact paper on the shelves. “Liners prevent damage to the wood and paint and make future clean-ups so much easier,” says Catherine Benson, a cleaning and organization aficionado based in Lexington, Kentucky.

Removing everything from the pantry will help you survey what you have in order to organize it better.

Before you return everything into the pantry, group items by category. There are several ways to do this, and experts recommend choosing the method that best suits you. One idea is to group like items together. “Think of your pantry as your own personal grocery store—canned goods together, pastas together, baking ingredients together,” Barnhart shares.

Another option is to categorize items by how you shop and plan meals. “If you shop with specific meals in mind and like to meal plan, group those ingredients together; for example, create a dinner zone that includes individual categories or bins such as pasta, grains, and soup,” says Lisa Eckerle, a professional organizer and owner of The Designer Organizer. If you shop by stocking up on pantry goods, categories like canned goods, baking supplies, and condiments may make more sense. “We normally use a hybrid approach for most of our clients, creating zones based on activity and categories within the zones based on food type,” Eckerle shares.

Once you’ve organized your categories, you might want containers to hold them. But before purchasing any storage vessels, measure pantry shelves, noting their width, depth, and height. Barnhart and Eckerle recommend incorporating the following storage solutions to maximize space and add style.

Risers are one of Barnhart’s favorite ways to store canned goods. “It makes it much easier to see the canned items in the back as well as what is in the front, and I feel it also helps avoid over-buying or repurchasing because you can see what you actually have,” she says.

Turntables are a must-have for pro organizers. “With all L-shaped pantries, we always start by placing turntables in most of the corners; these help maximize that space, avoid food getting lost or spoiled in the back, and create a cohesive visual,” Eckerle says. She notes they also work well on pantry shelves above eye level.

Consider containers and other tools to help store items in your pantry more effectively.

Turntables are great for oils and vinegars, sauces, condiments, broths, and spices. “If you have items you use daily, like nut butters, honey, and spreads that do not require refrigeration, consider putting those items on their own lazy Susan as well; it makes it easy to grab what you need and also makes it easy to clean up small spills and drips because they are contained to the lazy Susan,” Barnhart says.

Barnhart suggests using beautiful baskets or clear containers to group together things like snacks and dry goods. “This contains the items so they are not spilling out onto the shelves or floor and it is also much more aesthetically appealing as well,” Barnhart says.

One of Eckerle’s favorite recent hacks are wire cooling racks on the interior bottom of wooden storage bins. “By adding a plastic shelf liner under the cooling rack for easy cleaning, we created a unique fruit bin that was able to match the rest of the pantry’s decor and still store the fruit correctly with proper airflow,” she shares.

Now it’s time to add everything back into the pantry. “The most-reached-for categories should be near the door or center, with back stock and lesser-used category items placed in the back or the sides,” Eckerle says. She suggests putting meal-related items in the most accessible location, especially breakfast items, so they’re easy to grab when you’re in a rush.

Avoid storing seldom-used or heavy, small appliances on the top shelf or floor. “To prevent injury, damage, and frustration, those items should be stored between knee and shoulder height,” Eckerle says. Additionally, consider at what height you want each category. For example, “whether you want items out of reach of young children or dogs, or accessible and at eye level for children,” Eckerle says.

Keep things you grab often towards the front, while less-used items can go in the back.

“I am a big fan of labeling in the pantry—it helps systems stay in place when everyone knows what goes where and where to put it back,” Barnhart says. A label maker works great for this, but even stickers and sharpies will do.

Once you know how to organize a kitchen pantry, it’s important to maintain it. Eckerle recommends lightly resetting the pantry after every grocery haul. Additionally, she advises scheduling a day each quarter for a thorough pantry reset. “Re-check expiration dates, dispose of open food, and throw away or donate the items/categories that are no longer on your menu,” she says. You can also use this time to consider any seasonal menu changes that may impact how you organize your pantry. “Depending on the season, you may purchase different ingredients or cook different types of meals,” says Shweta Thota, a lifestyle content creator and Intel hardware engineer based in Sacramento. “This may require rearranging your pantry to accommodate seasonal items.” For example, in the winter, you may want to have a setup that works for more canned goods.
