#4837. Zinc: The Missing Link in Anorexia?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Over more than three decades of treating children, adolescents, and adults with eating disorders—including anorexia nervosa—I’ve seen the same pattern again and again. A patient arrives with severe anorexia, and they turn out to be severely deficient in one essential mineral: zinc.

So, while anorexia is a complicated disease, one part of treatment is very simple: If you, your child, or your patient has anorexia, the first and best step toward recovery may be correcting a zinc deficiency.

1: Zinc deficiency looks remarkably like anorexia. Imagine I described someone with a poor appetite, weight loss, slowed growth, changes in taste and smell, depression, anxiety, problems concentrating, low energy, social withdrawal, and digestive complaints. Would you think I was describing anorexia nervosa? You’d be right.

But I’d also be describing the symptoms of…zinc deficiency. Yes, many of the hallmark symptoms of anorexia are also classic symptoms of zinc deficiency. That doesn’t prove zinc deficiency causes anorexia. But it raises an obvious question: Could at least some of what we’ve traditionally thought of as the symptoms of anorexia actually be driven—or made worse—by a deficiency of this one nutrient?

2: Zinc deficiency is extremely common in people with anorexia. When researchers measure zinc levels in people with anorexia, they consistently find that a substantial percentage are deficient. Depending on the study and the methods used, at least half—and in some studies many more—show evidence of inadequate zinc status.

3: Remove zinc from an animal’s diet—and it begins to resemble someone with anorexia. In several studies, when scientists fed laboratory animals a diet lacking zinc, the animals ate less and lost weight. Growth slowed. They became less active socially. Females stopped reproducing. In short, they displayed features of anorexia nervosa.

Zinc is involved in hundreds of biological processes throughout the body; it helps regulate the activity of more than 300 enzymes, and it influences thousands of proteins that control growth, repair, metabolism, and communication between cells. In terms of our understanding of anorexia, zinc is crucial for:

Appetite regulation. Zinc participates in the complex network of hormones and signaling molecules that help regulate hunger, satiety, and energy balance. When zinc levels fall, that finely tuned system begins to malfunction. Appetite often declines. Food becomes less appealing. Eating can begin to feel like an obligation rather than a pleasure. This creates a cruel biological cycle.

A person who is already eating too little develops a zinc deficiency. The zinc deficiency further suppresses appetite. Reduced appetite leads to even less food intake. That, in turn, worsens the zinc deficiency.

I’ve seen this cycle happen so many times that I now think of it as one of the central biological engines driving anorexia. Breaking this cycle is one of the reasons correcting zinc deficiency can be so important.

Intra-brain communication. Zinc helps regulate the activity of several neurotransmitter systems that have long been implicated in anorexia, including glutamate and GABA, while also influencing serotonin and other chemical messengers involved in mood and anxiety.

You may be thinking: The biological connection between zinc deficiency and anorexia certainly sounds convincing. But does correcting the deficiency actually help people recover?

For more than four decades, studies on zinc and anorexia point in the same general direction: When people with anorexia receive supplemental zinc, they tend to improve. They gain weight more readily. Their appetite and sense of taste may return. Their mood becomes more stable. Physical development resumes. And, importantly, zinc has generally proved safe and well-tolerated.

One of the most impressive clinical trials enrolled 35 women who had been hospitalized with anorexia. Each patient was randomly assigned to receive either 100 milligrams (mg) of zinc daily or a placebo. The women continued taking zinc or a placebo until they achieved a 10% increase in body mass index (BMI). The results were striking.

The women receiving zinc increased their BMI at twice the rate of those receiving the placebo. Think about what that means. Both groups were hospitalized. Both were receiving expert care for anorexia. Both were working to regain weight. The principal difference between the two groups was that one also received zinc. And that group recovered significantly faster.

Writing in The International Journal of Eating Disorders, the researchers concluded, ‘‘The use of zinc supplementation should be considered in the treatment of AN patients.’’ I agree.

You’ll find citations to many other similarly impressive studies in the references at the end of this blog. The overall message from the research is that correcting zinc deficiency can improve recovery from anorexia nervosa.

Unlike vitamin C or niacin deficiency, zinc deficiency doesn’t cause one distinct, readily diagnosable disease. Instead, it can produce a wide and seemingly unrelated assortment of physical and psychological problems. These can include:

To complicate matters, normal blood zinc does not always mean normal zinc status—because only a tiny fraction of the body’s zinc circulates freely in the blood, and the body works hard to maintain adequate zinc in the bloodstream.

For these reasons, laboratory results must be interpreted in context. A zinc value near the lower end of the reference range may be particularly significant when it appears alongside anorexia, restrictive eating, poor appetite, altered taste, slow healing, frequent infection, anxiety, depression, or other signs associated with deficiency.

Once zinc deficiency has been identified—or is strongly suspected—the next step is correcting it. I generally recommend beginning with therapeutic doses as part of a comprehensive program of targeted nutritional therapy. My protocols are the following:

For adolescents, the typical starting dose is 15 mg of zinc twice daily, for a daily total of 30 mg.

For adults, the typical starting dose is 30 mg twice daily, for a daily total of 60 mg.

After approximately three months, these doses are generally reduced by half—to 15 mg daily for adolescents, and 30 mg daily for adults. This level establishes ongoing maintenance of zinc levels during recovery.

These recommendations should be individualized for the patient. The protocol should also be supervised by a qualified healthcare professional knowledgeable about nutritional medicine.

You can read much more about zinc and anorexia in my new book, Finally Nourished: A Science-Based Plan to Correct Malnutrition in Anorexia Nervosa—and Achieve True and Lasting Recovery.

Kawamoto JC, et al. Age, sex and reproductive status alter the severity of anorexia in zinc deficient rats. Physiology & Behavior. 1986 Oct;38(4):485-93

Rains TM, et al. Food intake patterns are altered during long-term zinc deficiency in rats. Physiology & Behavior. 1998 Dec 1;65(3):473-8.

#4836. Hormone Therapy May Help Improve Menopause Brain Fog, Mood Changes

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Menopause hormone therapy (MHT), also known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), helps manage various menopause symptoms.

Currently, MHT is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help relieve hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, and dyspareunia (pain during sex).

However, recent research has found that MHT may also help improve mental symptoms like “brain fog” and mood changes.

Other research also found that MHT does not affect dementia risk. This research followed the FDA’s removal of the black box warning on these products, which suggested they may increase the risk.

Together, these studies show that MHT may help people experiencing menopause in ways not previously realized and that it is generally safe to use.

Research published in Scientific Reports on September 1 suggests that an estrogen hormone treatment that combines estriol and progesterone may help ease the symptoms of brain fog during menopause.

Brain fog may involve memory lapses, difficulty concentrating, and slower thinking.

Just about two-thirds of women experience cognitive difficulties, like brain fog, during the menopausal transition. However, there is currently no Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- approved treatment for these symptoms.

This study was an observational case series that followed 20 menopausal women with an average age of 53. Each participant was given a baseline assessment for cognitive symptoms prior to treatment.

They were then treated for 12 months with a customized regimen of estriol and progesterone.

Estriol is a natural form of estrogen that occurs during pregnancy and has been used in Europe and Asia to treat other symptoms of menopause.

After 12 months, the participants reported significant reductions in:

“Estrogen plays a well-documented role in protecting the brain, yet there are still no approved type and dose of treatment that specifically targets the cognitive symptoms so many women experience during menopause,” Rhonda Voskuhl, MD, neurologist, member of the Comprehensive Menopause Center at UCLA Health, and senior study author, said in a press release.

“Women are often told to simply live with brain fog, when in fact there is a neuroscience basis for it, and potentially a way to address it. That gap in care is what motivated us to look more closely at estriol,” Voskuhl said.

This was a small, preliminary case series without a placebo group or randomization. More research is needed to confirm the benefits for cognitive symptoms.

A study published September 9 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society, showed that hormone therapy may help improve mood changes in women in midlife.

The researchers noted that mood disturbances, such as depression, irritability, anxiety, and mental exhaustion, affect up to 68% of women during menopause.

“The erratic changes and loss of estrogen associated with this hormonal transition can lower serotonin and dopamine levels, which [are] associated with depression and cognitive changes, including poor concentration, brain fog, and memory loss,” said Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included 260 individuals with an average age of 52 years. Just over half of the participants had a history of anxiety or depression, and 24% were using an antidepressant medication at the start of the study.

Each participant completed the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) both before and after initiating hormone therapy for FDA-approved indications, such as hot flashes and night sweats.

The average follow-up during the study was 4.5 months. Between the baseline and the follow-up, there was a significant reduction in the MRS psychological scores. The percentage of participants with severe mood symptoms decreased from 62.3% to 24.6%.

Treatment response didn’t appear to differ by age, menopausal stage, psychiatric history, or antidepressant use. These findings suggest that hormone therapy may help improve mood symptoms in midlife, especially for those with higher severity of symptoms before treatment.

“This study supports the evidence that starting hormone therapy for the typical disruptive symptoms of menopause may bring collateral benefits, including improvement in mood,” Ross said. “Communicating with your healthcare provider is always best to manage your symptoms and prepare yourself properly for this next stage of life.”

For decades, women have been warned about the serious potential risks associated with menopause hormone therapy (MHT). This included an FDA “black box” warning citing complications like cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

However, a recent meta-analysis commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO) that included data from more than a million women, and was published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, found that MHT neither increased nor decreased dementia risk.

“The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia,” Melissa Melville, a PhD candidate and aging researcher in the Department of Clinical Health Psychology at the University College London, and first author of the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

In the same interview, Melville stressed that the importance of this work is twofold: for clinicians, there is an urgent need for higher-quality research, and for patients, decisions about MHT should be guided by symptoms and well-established benefits and risks.

#4835. Korean police book 80 Tesla drivers over illegal FSD unlock devices

Seoul police have booked 80 people for using aftermarket devices to switch on Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” in cars that aren’t allowed to run it in South Korea. Officers also seized 21 of the devices.

The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency announced the case on Tuesday. It’s the largest enforcement action yet against the FSD “jailbreak” hardware that has spread through China, Europe, and Korea over the past year.

Police say the suspects either imported the unlock modules from Europe and China or made their own. One plugged a European-made unit into his own Tesla. Another, an IT worker, built his device with information he found on GitHub.

Suspects also swapped advice online on how to unlock FSD and how to stop the car from keeping any record that it had been activated.

They’re charged under Korea’s Motor Vehicle Management Act, which bans unauthorized software changes that can affect a vehicle’s safety. The penalty is up to two years in prison or a fine of up to 20 million won (about $15,000).

The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport asked police to look into it back in April after finding signs of unauthorized activation. A police official told Korea JoongAng Daily that “safety risks were confirmed,” including the possibility of FSD misreading driving conditions. The investigation is ongoing, with police consulting the ministry and the Korea Transportation Safety Authority on the technical side.

Tesla launched FSD (Supervised) in South Korea in late 2025, but only on US-built vehicles: Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck. Those cars are exempt from Korean safety certification under the Korea-US free trade agreement. The Model 3 and Model Y, which Tesla ships to Korea from Giga Shanghai, haven’t cleared Korea’s safety standards for the feature.

And those two models are the bulk of the fleet. Citing Carisyou Data Lab, Korea JoongAng Daily reports that 47,458 of the 229,311 Teslas on Korean roads as of August, or 20.7%, can legally use FSD.

That number doesn’t match the government’s own count from a few months earlier. In May, data released by lawmaker Park Yong-gap showed just 4,292 of 180,684 registered Teslas (2.4%) were eligible: 2,708 Model X, 1,193 Model S, and 391 Cybertruck. Either way, the vast majority of Korean Tesla owners can’t legally use FSD, and some of them paid over $6,000 for it anyway.

The hardware is the same, which is why the hack works. The modules plug into the car’s CAN bus and get around the regional software lock.

Tesla has been fighting the devices itself. In April, it started remotely detecting them and stripping FSD from affected cars, warned owners they’d be fully liable for any crash and could lose warranty coverage, and permanently banned some Chinese owners from FSD.

Tesla & Starlink: The reality as reported in 2021: every one of our Tesla autos are connected 24/7/365 to the company. It was that year that a programming glitch came where some vehicles would not function. That was quickly corrected. In the news today where proof that when Elon shut down Starlink to Ukraine, russian missiles came and killed 5 people, including one baby. ... here is the reality you and me must face: Musk holds the power right now, that if he decides he does not like 'some owners' of Teslas, he can SHUT DOWN instantly those vehicles from moving. It is not enough that potentially, every conversation and communication device used inside those vehicles 'can' be recorded but, as he has proven perfectly willing to do to Ukraine families, so he could at any moment 'shut down' some specific users of Tesla vehicles at-will. this is not hype, fantasy or gusswork. This is how the online active update software communications system works on every car we buy from Tesla. My company is looking into other providers of Sat-Com services, and we are re-evaluating our own vehicle choices.

It’s easy to see why people do this. Picture a Korean owner of a Shanghai-built Model Y who paid for FSD, watching the Model X next door run the same software on the same computer. That’s frustrating.

Tesla sold FSD to owners of cars it had no regulatory path to enable in Korea, the same way it sold “Full Self-Driving” in Europe for years while approval kept slipping. It only dropped the name there this month after Germany pushed back. Sell a feature people can’t legally use and you create the market for the jailbreak.

Korea has now shown it will actually prosecute. So will Tesla refund the Korean owners who bought a feature their cars may never be allowed to run?

#4834. Sykeruns X7 electric dirt bike review: A lot of power for surprisingly little money

The mini electric dirt bike market has exploded over the last few years, with seemingly countless new brands offering everything from pint-sized electric pit bikes to surprisingly powerful off-road machines. The Sykeruns X7 falls somewhere in the middle, offering enough power to get into some serious trouble while keeping the price relatively approachable.

I’ve spent some time now riding the X7, and while it certainly isn’t the most refined electric dirt bike I’ve tested, there’s enough to like about what you’re getting for the money.

In fact, if you’re looking for a reasonably powerful electric dirt bike for recreational trail riding without spending several thousand dollars, this might be worth a closer look.

The Sykeruns X7 is a compact electric dirt bike featuring a 5,500W peak-rated motor, which translates to around 7.4 horsepower. That’s quite a bit of power for a bike at this price point of $1,699, especially considering that many similarly priced electric two-wheelers are significantly less powerful. Oh, and for our readers, we’ve gotten you set up with a 20% discount. Just use code ELECTREK20 to drop the price down to an impressive $1,359!

Sykeruns claims a top speed of 57 mph (92 km/h), though since this is an off-road only bike, you’ll rarely get the chance to put that claim to the test. I certainly didn’t, as I didn’t have a long enough and flat enough stretch of trail where I felt comfortable hitting nearly highway speeds on a low-cost e-moto.

The battery is a 60V 27Ah pack, providing 1,620 Wh of capacity. Sykeruns claims up to 60 miles (96 km) of range, though as with virtually every electric dirt bike, your actual range will depend heavily on how aggressively you’re riding. Fast trail riding, steep climbs, and repeated hard acceleration can eat through battery capacity much more quickly than leisurely cruising. Suffice it to say that you’ll likely not see the 60 mile figure in real world scenarios, but that’s still a fairly large battery.

The bike rolls on a 17-inch front wheel and 14-inch rear wheel, both wrapped in knobby off-road tires. Hydraulic disc brakes handle stopping duties, while an inverted suspension fork and rear monoshock help smooth out the bumps.

At 143 lb (65 kg), the X7 isn’t exactly featherweight, but it’s also far from being a full-size electric motorcycle.

The first thing I was surprised about with the X7 is that it offers a pretty decent amount of performance for the money. There’s enough power here to have some real fun, and the bike doesn’t feel like one of those underpowered mini electric motorcycles that struggles once you get beyond casual neighborhood speeds.

That said, I wouldn’t describe the acceleration as mind-blowing, either. We’re not talking about the kind of explosive power delivery you’d get from a high-end electric dirt bike costing several times as much. Instead, the X7 delivers a healthy amount of acceleration that feels appropriate for a recreational off-road machine.

And let’s be real here, that’s probably what most people shopping in this budget category are looking for.

The suspension is another area where the X7 earns a passing grade without necessarily winning any awards. The front fork and rear shock do their jobs, absorbing the bumps and ruts you’d expect to encounter on typical trails. It’s nothing I’d call plush, but I could see it doing light jumps with minimal air time.

Would I want to take this thing to a motocross track and start launching it off massive jumps? Not particularly. The suspension doesn’t have the premium feel or sophisticated damping of more expensive machines.

But for general trail riding, exploring dirt roads, and the occasional overlanding shenanigans, it’s perfectly serviceable. Not every electric dirt bike needs to be a competition-ready machine, and the X7 seems comfortable occupying that more recreational category.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the tires, which seem well suited to the bike’s intended purpose. The knobby tread offers a reasonable amount of grip for off-road riding, and I didn’t find myself immediately wishing for a tire upgrade.

The overall size is worth mentioning, too. This isn’t a particularly large electric dirt bike, but at my modest 5’7” (170 cm) height, I felt comfortable on it. The riding position didn’t feel overly cramped, and the bike was manageable enough that I didn’t feel like I was wrestling with an oversized machine.

Taller riders might find it a bit more compact than they’d prefer, but for average-height riders, the proportions seem reasonable.

If there’s one area where the X7 reminds you of its budget-friendly $1,699 price tag, it’s the overall level of refinement.

Nothing about the bike struck me as particularly premium. The components, finishes, and general construction are more in line with what I’d expect from a relatively inexpensive electric dirt bike.

But that’s not necessarily a criticism. There’s a difference between something feeling inexpensive and something feeling inadequate, and the X7 generally stays on the acceptable side of that line.

The controls are straightforward, the digital display provides the basic information you need, and the overall package feels focused on delivering usable performance rather than impressing riders with fancy features.

The grippy hydraulic brakes are also a welcome inclusion, especially considering the speeds this bike is capable of reaching. With a machine that can approach highway speeds, having proper motorcycle-style braking hardware is important.

Of course, long-term durability is a separate question. Budget electric dirt bikes don’t always have the same track record, parts availability, or established dealer networks as the more recognizable motorcycle brands. That’s something worth considering before purchasing, particularly if you plan to ride hard or frequently.

One thing I appreciate about the Sykeruns X7 is that the company makes its intended use fairly clear.

There’s a large red warning sticker on the bike explaining that it’s intended for off-road use only. That’s a good thing, especially in today’s market, where the lines between electric bicycles, electric dirt bikes, and electric motorcycles are becoming increasingly blurred, despite laws existing to keep these types of bikes out of the bike lane and off of public roads.

The X7 is absolutely not an electric bicycle. It doesn’t have pedals, it produces several thousand watts of power, and it’s capable of speeds far beyond anything permitted under electric bicycle regulations.

It’s an off-road electric motorcycle, plain and simple.

Interestingly, though, Sykeruns has equipped the bike with features like a tail light and turn signals, which could potentially give some riders the wrong impression.

Those are certainly useful features on a motorcycle, but they don’t magically make a vehicle street legal. Without the necessary certification, registration, and other road-use requirements, the X7 remains an off-road-only machine.

I worry that some buyers might see those lights and assume they can ride the bike around town like a small electric motorcycle. That’s not the case, and it’s important to understand that distinction before buying one.

After spending time with the Sykeruns X7, my biggest takeaway is that this is a reasonably capable electric dirt bike at a pretty compelling price.

It’s not the best electric dirt bike I’ve ever ridden. The suspension is fairly basic, the build quality is unremarkable, and there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about the design.

But for $1,699 (or $1,359 if you use the code ELECTREK20 to take 20% off!), you’re getting a 5.5 kW peak-rated electric motorcycle with a sizable battery, proper off-road tires, hydraulic brakes, and enough performance to have some genuine fun on the trails.

I wouldn’t say that the X7 here is trying to compete with more up-market electric dirt bikes from the likes of Juiced, Sur-Ron or Talaria on overall refinement, but they make this type of riding much more accessible.

And that’s really where I think the X7 makes the most sense.

If you’re an experienced dirt bike rider looking for a highly refined machine with excellent suspension and premium components, you’ll probably want to keep shopping.

But if you’re someone who wants a fun electric dirt bike for exploring private property, cruising around trails where motorized riding is permitted, or just enjoying some recreational off-road riding without spending a fortune, the Sykeruns X7 offers a pretty reasonable package.

It doesn’t need to be amazing at everything. At this price, being pretty good at most things is already an accomplishment.

#4833. Heart Failure Is Becoming More Common in Adults Under 65, Report Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023, more than double the number in 1990, according to a new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analysis published September 30 in JAMA Cardiology.

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Despite its name, heart failure doesn’t mean the heart has stopped beating.

A separate 2026 report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) found that heart failure contributed to more than 450,000 deaths in the United States in 2023, with particularly sharp increases in mortality among adults under 65.

Approximately 7.7 million U.S. adults (3%) are living with heart failure, according to the HFSA report. That number is projected to rise to 8.7 million by 2030, 10.3 million by 2040, and 11.4 million by 2050.

The GBD researchers said the findings highlight the growing burden of heart failure associated with population growth and aging, as well as the need for prevention and treatment strategies targeting common causes such as ischemic heart disease and hypertension (high blood pressure).

Between 2010 and 2022, heart failure hospitalization rates increased among adults under 65 while declining among those 65 and older. Between 2001 and 2020, estimated heart failure mortality rates more than doubled among adults ages 25 to 44 and nearly doubled among those ages 45 to 64.

“I think we’re seeing the impact of cardiovascular risk factors developing earlier in life. Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea are affecting younger adults at higher rates than in previous generations,” Kevin Shah, MD, Program Director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the analysis, told Healthline.

“When those risk factors are present for decades, they can eventually lead to heart failure at a younger age,” he said.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist at Manhattan Cardiology in New York City who was also not involved in the analysis, noted that improvements in early detection may also play a role.

“Our tools to detect early heart failure are also improving with time, and as a result, patients may receive an earlier diagnosis and can hopefully start medical therapy to prevent progression or possibly even reverse the process entirely.”

Heart failure contributed to 452,573 deaths in the United States in 2023, accounting for approximately 14.6% of all deaths that year, according to the HFSA report.

Age-adjusted heart failure mortality rates increased by approximately 37% between 2010 and 2023, with preliminary 2024 data suggesting the upward trend is continuing.

This increase appears to have reversed more than a decade of previous progress in reducing heart failure mortality.

Ischemic heart disease and hypertension were among the most common causes of heart failure in older adults, according to the GBD report. However, the underlying causes varied considerably by age group and region.

Among children and young adults, congenital heart abnormalities and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common causes of heart failure. Heart failure associated with alcohol use was most prevalent during middle adulthood.

The analysis also identified regional differences in the underlying causes of heart failure:

The global burden of heart failure is expected to grow as populations age.

While not all cases of heart failure can be prevented, managing certain risk factors can help reduce your risk. These include:

According to Shah, other important steps to help prevent heart failure include maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, and managing conditions such as diabetes and high cholesterol.

He added that regular medical care is important because many of these risk factors can be identified and treated long before heart failure develops.

“Heart failure is often treatable and may even be reversible with early diagnosis and treatment. It is important for patients to seek help early if they have concerning symptoms, such as exertional shortness of breath, chest pain, leg swelling, or anything else they’re concerned about. Talk with your doctors early and often,” said Blumfield.

#4832. A Meeting With Elizabeth Holmes

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Like many Americans, I recently watched You Can See Everything, the documentary that follows Elizabeth Holmes through the weeks before she reported to prison. I left the theater fascinated and bewildered. Throughout the movie, I kept asking the same question the filmmakers seem to be asking: Am I being deceived, or am I missing something because I don't know enough?

I have asked myself that question about Holmes before. In July 2013, I was the Deputy Commissioner for the New York City Health Department, where I oversaw the city's infectious disease programs and the public health laboratory. City Hall asked me to meet with a promising new lab-testing company; a few weeks later, I joined an hour-long video call with Holmes, her team, and our lab director.

I still have my notes. Holmes and her colleagues told us that their company, Theranos, had developed a more convenient way to test blood in small amounts that would cut testing costs by 30 percent.

A wide range of tests had been validatedFederal and New York State regulatory approvals were completeThey secured a Department of Defense contract. Testing was scheduled to launch at New York Walgreens pharmacies within months.

My colleague and I asked repeatedly about the underlying science and data. Every time, we got the same answer: they could not disclose business secrets, but everything worked and was approved. Rest assured.

When the call ended, my colleague and I were dumbfounded. Nothing we knew about collecting specimens, validating tests, or getting regulatory approval made their story plausible. And yet I doubted myself. Holmes spoke with such composure and certainty and had such powerful connections and investors that I kept wondering: Did she know something about science or lab regulations that I didn't?

We offered to evaluate the device in our lab before any wider use. Neither side ever followed up. When the Wall Street Journal published its first investigation into the company in October 2015, I called my colleague, and we both said the same thing: "We knew it!" Most of what she said in that meeting was not true.

After watching the movie, I kept thinking about that incident and how it raised a hard healthcare problem: knowing when to trust your own expertise and when to defer to someone else's.

We assume that people who sound certain know more than we do. This is particularly common when checking a person’s claims is difficult or costly. That describes the Theranos meeting almost exactly. We could not check her claims because she said her data was confidential, and she spoke with absolute certainty.

While the lack of data made me suspicious, I fell prey to something known as “the halo effect,” where people with credibility in one domain are often thought to be credible experts in other domains. Theranos had funders and board members who had extremely prestigious backgrounds in government and the military. Even though none of them had a background in laboratory medicine, I assumed they had done sufficient due diligence on the technology.

A big challenge in health: The body is so complex that none of us can be experts in everything. As a physician, if I order an MRI on a patient, I rely on the radiologist to interpret it correctly. When I order a blood test, I rely on laboratory technicians to use validated methods and equipment. I could not do my job if I had to personally verify that everyone knows what they are doing and is doing it correctly. The need to trust others is even greater for patients, because most of them will not be medical experts.

The problem, of course, is that humans are imperfect. Medical errors are, unfortunately, quite common. Someone did something wrong—errors of commission; someone forgot to do something—errors of omission. And, because medical knowledge is always growing, something correct 10 years ago may be incorrect now. I always encourage people to ask their healthcare providers questions and, with major health decisions, to seek second opinions.

How do you decide when and whom to trust? Here are a few questions you can ask whether you are a patient talking to a doctor or interpreting health claims online.

First, is this an area where you have real knowledge and experience? If so, give your own judgment more weight than you are inclined to, even when the person across from you is more confident than you are.

Second, does their authority come from the relevant field? A famous name, a large social media following, or impressive business credentials do not mean they understand how a vaccine works or what a blood test measures.

Third, is the other person offering evidence or only certainty? Consider asking, “What is the evidence that supports this approach? Is this what expert guidelines recommend?” Trustworthy experts can explain their reasoning or point you to high-quality studies or published guidelines to check their claims.

Fourth, has anyone independently checked? Has it been approved by the FDA or another government regulatory agency? Or do major professional organizations recommend it?

We need our health experts and institutions to see everything—the methods and the data—to make sure medications, vaccines, and other health interventions are safe and effective. But when someone asks for our trust and won’t back it up with data, we need to consider trusting our own judgment or asking for a second opinion.

#4830. Postpartum Prevention Plan: Time Outside, Exercise, Socialize

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Postpartum depression and anxiety are major issues that affect new caregivers. Many new parents focus on the birth plan to prepare for this major stage of life. But what I find in my work as a clinical psychologist is that new families really benefit from a postpartum plan as well. What are the needs, relationships, and activities that will help you maintain your well-being postpartum? Knowing these will promote your child’s well-being as well. I developed the following mnemonic to capture core helpful practices that are supported by research: Time Outside, Exercise, and Socialize. These three practices can provide a daily structure that maximizes joy during a time that is challenging but also fulfilling.

1. Time Outside: Follow the mantra often told to caregivers of newborns — leave the house every day. Time spent in nature has been associated with enhanced mood, emotional regulation, optimism, resilience, and child development (Hall et al., 2023). Research on mothers and nature has attested to the benefits of the outdoors on postnatal well-being and the relief it provides from indoor stressors (Hall et al., 2023). Getting out is key. Even if being in nature isn't possible, go out for coffee, lunch, or to a museum to provide novelty and stimulation that can vary your routine and perk up the day. Physicians have dispelled myths that you shouldn’t leave home with your newborn, as fresh air and a change of scenery are beneficial to both parent and child well-being (Davis, 2015).

2. Exercise: If you are able to, getting some kind of walk in every day with a newborn is not only good for you but also for your child. Strap them into a carrier of your choosing or affix a stroller with all the things you might need to leave the house for a stretch. A meta-analysis reviewing a wide range of studies found that exercise alone (without the use of other interventions) is effective in reducing postpartum depression and anxiety (Deprato et al., 2025). A moderate reduction in the severity of symptoms was achieved through at least 80 minutes a week of rigorous exercise, which could include a brisk walk, swimming, cycling, and other activities.

3. Socialize: Invite a friend or family member for a visit or walk. Attend a local baby-friendly gathering that can take you and an infant out into the world, like a yoga, music, play, or story time group. Research suggests that social interaction is a powerful protective factor in preventing postpartum depression and anxiety (Feinberg et al., 2022). Another study found that social support is particularly important for women who are at risk of postpartum mental health problems, such as those with more than one child, pregnancy loss, negative body image, and a history of mental health problems.

It is important to note that all three of these components overlap — socializing, time outside, and exercise could all take place during a long walk with a friend. But if you are having trouble getting out with the baby, have others help you, if possible, so you don’t have to make this happen on your own. And if consistent practice of these activities doesn’t seem to help, reaching out to a medical and/or mental health professional is essential. Severe cases of postpartum depression and anxiety may not remit with daily health behaviors, but require professional treatment, which can be very effective. More support is available at the National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-852-6262) and Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773).

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

Davis, S. (2015). Can I take my newborn outside? https://www.webmd.com/parenting/baby/features/can-i-take-my-newborn-outside

Deprato, A., Ruchat, S. M., Ali, M. U., Cai, C., Forte, M., Gierc, M., Meyer, S., Sjwed, T. N., Shirazi, S., Matenchuk, B. A., Jones, P. A. T., Sivak, A., & Davenport, M. H. (2025). Impact of postpartum physical activity on maternal depression and anxiety: A systematic review and meta-analysis. #4829. BMW is going upscale with its first 3-row EV, the iX7

BMW’s next electric SUV won’t just be bigger. The iX7 will sit at the top of the brand’s EV lineup when it debuts in 2027, bringing a more luxurious option to the mix.

After the new X5 and iX5, the X7, BMW’s biggest SUV, is due for a Neue Klasse overhaul. BMW said the second-generation X7 will arrive in 2027, including the first fully electric version, the iX7.

Ahead of its upcoming debut, camouflaged prototypes have been spotted testing, revealing a few design changes.

Although it won’t fully adopt BMW’s Neue Klasse design, like the iX3, the three-row SUV appears to feature a slimmer, more upright Kidney Grille instead of the traditional wide BMW Grille.

The iX7 also swaps conventional pull-style door handles for small handles on the vehicle’s pillar. It also retains split headlights rather than the updated Neue Klasse-style headlights on the iX3 (shown below on the right).

While BMW has yet to reveal details, a Reddit user who claims to work at BMW’s factory in South Carolina and has seen the second-generation X7 shared a few new details.

Like the X5 and iX5, the new X7 and iX7 will retain a more traditional design rather than going full-on Neue Klasse, including the Kidney Grille. The user also said BMW is dropping the split tailgate, which it did with the new X5, in favor of a standard one-piece tailgate.

Inside, the dashboard and center console are similar to the new X5, but with upgraded tech and features from the new 7 Series sedan.

BMW said the new 7 Series sedan “takes the lead when it comes to the introduction of technologies from the Neue Klasse into existing models.”

Optional features will reportedly include the upgraded 31.3″ 8K BMW Theatre Screen for rear passengers and a 14.6″ BMW Passenger Screen. It will also have optional touch screen panels on the rear doors, the user said.

While most of the claims make sense, we’ll have to wait for BMW to confirm it officially. The new X7 and iX7 are expected to debut in mid-2027.

Like the iX5 60 xDrive, the three-row iX7 is expected to use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. The iX5’s AWD setup delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, enabling it to hit 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.

The iX5 uses a massive 144 kWh battery, which BMW said offers up to 435 miles of range. It will also use an 800V electrical system for fast charging.

BMW showed just how fast it can charge during a media event in Southern California earlier this month, where the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW. With up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes, BMW says.

The new X7 and iX7 are expected to go into production at BMW’s Spartanburg plant in SC in late 2027, joining the new iX5.

#4828. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

#4827. A Billion More Dark-Morning Commutes

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 4, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In July, my post about the big debate over yearly time changes described the position of professional sleep organizations that permanent standard time (ST) is more aligned with our circadian physiology than permanent daylight saving time (DST), or the alternating system we currently have in the U.S. (except in Arizona). As a member of one of those organizations, and having read their arguments, I am in favor of permanent standard time.

Since I posted, an interesting study was released to journalists on October 29, which estimated the number of dark-morning student-commutes to school we would see if the “Sunshine Protection Act” (proposing permanent DST) had been passed by the Senate and signed into law. Rodríguez Ferrante and colleagues at the University of Washington calculated that the number was around a billion. Central to their argument against permanent DST was their analysis of a decade of national fatal crash records, which found that there were higher odds of pedestrian involvement in dark-morning crashes than light-morning ones (odds ratio [OR] 1.77), and even higher odds for children aged 5–18 (OR 2.22). Safety for children waiting for the bus and riding to school in buses and cars was a primary concern of some senators.

How have you and your family adjusted to this fall's time change? As for myself, after four days, I still get sleepy earlier in the evening and wake up earlier. I am in the “elderly” demographic, and it seems that with older age comes slower adjustment by the circadian clock (Lombardi, 2025). Lombardi explains that infants and older persons have a harder time adjusting to time changes, and the article also describes the physiology that makes adjustment difficult for many of us. Typically "spring foward" is more difficult for evening types (owls) than for morning types (larks), since they have to adjust to getting up earlier.

I came across an interesting fact in an American history book. It stated that “On Tuesday, October 30, 1787, readers of a newspaper, the New York Packet, found on the front page an advertisement for an almanac that came bound with tables predicting the 'Rising and Setting of the Sun,' the 'Judgement of the Weather,' the 'Length of Days and Nights’…” (Lepore, 2018, p.xi.). This was, of course, Ben Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanac. And while other almanacs with such information were available in early America, Franklin’s was the most read secular book of the time (the Bible was first overall). It is interesting to ponder what Franklin would have thought about changing the clocks and which of the three most discussed alternatives he might have supported. Among his inventions was a clock, and I have no doubt that he could have altered it to automatically adjust for yearly time changes.

Lepore, J. (2018). These truths: A history of the United States. New York/London. W.W. Norton & Co.

Lombardi, P. (2025, December 13). How Long Does It Take to Adjust to Daylight Savings? Biology Insights. https://biologyinsights.com/how-long-does-it-take-to-adjust-to-daylight-savings/

Rodríguez Ferrante et al., Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for K–12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act, Current Biology (2026), in press. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.014

#4826. A Fun Way to Build Relational Skills

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Our relationships are the source of some of our greatest joys and deepest pain. When our relationships are thriving, we tend to thrive, and when they’re strained, we suffer. In fact, many of the most pressing problems, not only in our personal lives but also in the larger world, such as interpersonal abuse, war, racism, climate change, and animal exploitation, are driven by dysfunctional ways of relating: to other people, to animals and the environment, and even to ourselves. So building relational literacy—the understanding of and ability to practice healthy ways of relating—can help transform these problems.

Yet the people who most need to build relational literacy are also probably the least likely to pick up a self-help book or go to therapy. They may, however, happily spend an evening engrossed in a novel or bingeing on Netflix.

What if we could build relational skills through reading or watching enjoyable stories?

Stories, whether written or on-screen, teach us things, from how a courtroom works to what healthy communication looks like. Research suggests that stories also shape our beliefs and attitudes, for better or worse. And because every story features characters, and characters are always relating—to others, and at the very least to themselves—every story is teaching us how to relate. The only question is whether we’re learning skillful or harmful ways of relating.

Consider the all-too-common bar scene in which an affronted man “communicates with his fists” by beating up a stranger who was making eyes at his partner. Or the many revenge movies in which an aggrieved parent (often a father) seeks not only to catch, but to brutalize, the person who kidnapped their child. In contrast, series like This Is Us portray complex relationships and characters who are nuanced and vulnerable, who turn toward rather than against or away from each other, and who repair after a relational breach.

Stories can also help us recognize difficult-to-identify dynamics, such as those that arise with addiction or domestic abuse. We often see more clearly when we look at a situation from the outside, as observers of someone else’s experience. For example, the film When a Man Loves a Woman reveals how alcohol dependence impacts a family system, while the novel and movie It Ends With Us reveal how gaslighting and trauma bonding operate in an abusive relationship.

If you’re building relational skills through such means as reading nonfiction or taking courses, fiction can be a powerful supplement. Stories can bring the principles and tools described in nonfiction to life, showing what they look like and how they can be applied. This is why, after writing seven nonfiction books, several of which are about relationships, I wrote a novel. I wanted readers to be able to see relational concepts in action while also being entertained.

To get more out of novels and shows as tools for relational learning, you can use a list of questions for post-reading or -viewing. You can tailor the list to areas you want to grow in or concepts you’re learning through therapy or nonfiction (for example, attachment styles, relational repair, or the Gottmans’ “four horsemen”), and use it for personal reflection or for discussion with someone you’ve read or watched with.

You can start with questions like the following:

I’ve always believed that a great story leaves the reader or viewer a little better off than they were before. Whether you’re a therapist working with clients or an individual wanting to build your relational skills, consider adding stories to your relational toolkit. Stories not only teach us; they can help us have fun in the process of learning.

Braddock, K., & Dillard, J. P. (2016). Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors. Communication Monographs, 83(4), 446-467.

#4825. Waymo adds nearly 250 square miles of robotaxi coverage in 5 cities

Waymo is growing its driverless service area by nearly 250 square miles over the next week, spread across Los Angeles, Nashville, Orlando, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

That’s about as big as Tesla’s entire Houston Robotaxi geofence after this week’s expansion, and Waymo is adding it in cities where it already runs with nobody in the driver’s seat.

The company announced the expansion in a short post on its blog today. Here’s what changes in each market, with Waymo’s updated service area maps:

Service now runs down the coast into the South Bay, through Manhattan Beach and Redondo Beach to Torrance.

The zone pushes further south, and riders can now get to the zoo.

Coverage on the east side nearly doubles, and there’s more service downtown.

The service area now stretches north to La Jolla, taking in University City and Clairemont along the way.

Waymo is pushing further into the South Bay, including a connection to BART at Berryessa station in San Jose. The service area now runs from San Francisco down the Peninsula to San Jose and Campbell.

Waymo didn’t break out square mileage by city, and it didn’t say how many vehicles it’s adding to cover the new ground. The updated maps are already in the Waymo app.

Some of these markets are very young. Waymo opened Nashville to public riders in April with a zone of about 60 square miles covering downtown, Midtown, Music Row, and East Nashville. San Diego only went public on September 1, with roughly 50 square miles between the beach and I-15 that barely crossed north of I-8. So getting to La Jolla less than two months later is a big jump.

In May, Waymo pushed its coverage past 1,400 square miles across 11 cities, which is bigger than the state of Rhode Island. Since then, it went driverless in Las Vegas, launched San Diego, and now says it operates in 15 US metros with more than 500,000 paid rides per week. It’s even mapping Toronto for a 2028 launch.

Tesla is also drawing bigger maps. After launching Robotaxi in Dallas and Houston with tiny geofences in April, it stretched Houston to about 254 square miles this week, according to Robotaxi Tracker. But the tracker counts 34 vehicles in Houston.

I'd like to see Waymo add more airports to their service list. Airports are huge drivers of both ride count and revenue for ride services. Waymo currently serves airports in some of their cities, such as Phoenix, San Francisco, and Nashville. However, other major airports such as LAX, Atlanta, and Dallas/Fort Worth do not currently have terminal service even though Waymo operates in those cities. Adding these might not look flashy on a map, but it would be a huge addition to Waymo's bottom line.

And on the metric that reflects actual use, it’s not close. Waymo logged 3.9 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026, while Tesla’s driverless fleet did 558,000 miles in its latest reported week, mostly in Austin. That’s about 7x, and it comes on the same day Elon Musk claimed the robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest.”

I like this. Good progress. But I’ll be truly impressed when the Bay Area service area extends south into LA, expands north, and the same happens in San Diego.

It’s going to happen. Waymo is already dabbling with highway operations in California.I can see them linking all those service areas within the next 2 years. Maybe even by the end of next year if all goes well.

#4824. Happy for You, Sad for Me

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 5, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

If you’re struggling with infertility, you’ve likely experienced the pit-in-your-stomach sensation when someone close to you announces a pregnancy. You may simultaneously feel authentic joy for her and overwhelming grief for yourself. That sadness may turn to feelings of jealousy, anger, or even spite. While you don’t want anything horrible to happen to her, you may have fleeting thoughts of their pregnancy not working out. And then comes the guilt and self-doubt, asking yourself questions such as Am I a terrible person for having these thoughts?, What kind of friend am I?, and Why can't I just be happy for her?

Research shows that women struggling with infertility consistently experience envy of pregnant women and women with children, painful reactions to the pregnancies of friends and family members, negative self-comparisons, and withdrawal from situations that serve as reminders of their own struggles to conceive (Aiello et al., 2025).

Understanding what triggers these reactions can help you manage them with less guilt and without compromising your relationships or emotional well-being.

Give yourself permission to have two contradictory feelings at the same time. Being happy for someone else and feeling sad for yourself are not mutually exclusive. You can love your friend, want the very best for her, and still feel devastated by her pregnancy announcement. Often, it’s not really about her pregnancy at all, but rather a painful reminder of what you so desperately want and have invested so much of your time, energy, money, and hope into achieving.

The inability to be unconditionally supportive doesn't mean you're selfish or that you're not a good friend. It simply means you’re going through a devastating period in your life and that you want to experience the same joy as she gets to have.

It's natural to compare yourself with other people, particularly when they're reaching milestones you had hoped to achieve. During infertility, those comparisons can become difficult to escape when you are surrounded by pregnancy announcements, baby showers, first birthdays, and family photos. Staying connected to friends can be difficult when all they seem to talk about is their children, complain about sleepless nights, or announce they're expecting another baby. In fact, research shows that painful reminders, envy, negative self-comparison, and feelings of social exclusion and isolation are recurring themes in women's experiences of infertility (Aiello et al., 2025).

The hardest part may be the feeling that you are being left behind while everyone else's lives are moving forward. You may find that you start to measure your own losses against their milestones, remembering that a friend first got pregnant when you started your first IVF cycle or that another friend announced being pregnant with her second child as you were experiencing a pregnancy loss from a third transfer.

These comparisons can be particularly painful because infertility involves so much uncertainty. There's often no clear timeline, no guarantee of success, and very little control over the outcome.

Jealousy and envy are emotions most would rather not admit to experiencing because we want to think of ourselves as loving, generous, and supportive. Feeling jealous often leads to shame and self-loathing, which only compounds an already difficult life crisis.

But jealousy during infertility often has much more to do with your own sadness and disappointment than with resentment toward someone else. Infertility involves losses that aren't always visible or acknowledged by others. These intangible losses include an imagined timeline, the expectation of conceiving easily, or the sense of control you once had over your reproductive future.

You don't have to put yourself in a painful situation to show support or prove you're happy for someone else. You can skip a baby shower, avoid a family gathering, or mute someone's pregnancy updates on social media. And you don't have to explain or justify every one of these decisions.

There are ways to be supportive while also taking care of yourself: You can send a thoughtful card or gift without attending the baby shower. You can congratulate a friend and let her know that while you're happy for her, you may need a little space to navigate your own struggles. You can take a break from social media or leave a gathering early if it becomes overwhelming.

Research suggests that social withdrawal and feelings of being misunderstood are common experiences during infertility (Aiello et al., 2025). While avoiding certain situations may provide temporary relief, losing connections with people who care about you and have good intentions can make the infertility experience even lonelier.

Try to maintain relationships in which you feel understood and supported. That might mean spending time with friends who are sensitive to what you're going through, connecting with others experiencing infertility, joining a support group, or working with a mental health professional who understands reproductive mental health.

Imagine that a close friend who's just been through her fourth unsuccessful IVF cycle tells you that her sister, who wasn’t even trying to conceive, announced she's pregnant—and now she wants nothing to do with her. You probably wouldn't tell her that she's a horrible person for feeling this way. Instead, you would recognize how complicated the situation is, how much she's been through, and how painful this news might be for her.

Self-compassion means extending some of that same kindness and understanding to yourself. And research suggests that self-compassion matters. In a study of women undergoing infertility treatment, self-compassion was one of the pathways that contributed to psychological well-being (Chu et al., 2021).

So next time you want to berate yourself for having thoughts and feelings that feel negative, remind yourself that it's understandable to have a difficult reaction to something you've wanted so badly and recognize that you can care deeply about someone and still feel sad about your own circumstances. Sometimes it simply means allowing yourself to feel disappointed without judging yourself for it.

One of the hardest things about infertility is learning to live with emotions that don't always seem to fit together. You can feel hopeful and afraid, grateful and jealous, optimistic and discouraged. You can love the people around you and still find certain moments with them painful.

The next time someone announces a pregnancy and you find yourself struggling with a mixture of happiness, jealousy, sadness, and guilt, know that it’s a completely normal reaction to a difficult situation and try not to judge yourself. You can be happy for other people and acknowledge your own sadness at the same time. Sometimes, allowing yourself to feel what you feel, without adding guilt or shame, can make a difficult experience a little easier.

Aiello, A., Esplen, M. J., Boon, H., Zwingerman, R., Toner, B., & Maunder, R. G. (2025). A qualitative evidence synthesis of women’s experience of infertility and fertility treatment from an existential perspective. SAGE Open, 15. https://doi.org/10.1177/21582440251372769

Chu, X., Geng, Y., Zhang, R., & Guo, W. (2021). Perceived social support and life satisfaction in infertile women undergoing treatment: A moderated mediation model. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 651612.

#4823. Rivian electric van spotted in Walmart+ livery, hinting at a fleet deal

A Rivian electric delivery van wrapped in Walmart+ branding was photographed on a car hauler on I-94 in northwest Indiana today. It’s the first public sign that Walmart could become Rivian’s next big van customer after Amazon.

Neither company has announced a deal. But Walmart’s last two electric van suppliers are out of the business, and Rivian is one of the few companies still building a purpose-built electric delivery van in the US.

Reddit user biggie_ballzzz posted the photo to r/RIVNstock this afternoon, asking if anyone had heard about a partnership. The van is strapped to a multi-car trailer between two Ford pickups, with a big “Walmart+” logo on the side and “Same day. Right to your door.” on the rear doors.

There’s no mistaking the vehicle. It’s Rivian’s Commercial Van, with the same tall body and red light bar wrapping around the rear that you see on Amazon Prime vans everywhere.

A few commenters suspected an AI image, but there’s no clear evidence. In fact, a second commenter then shared a photo of a van in the same livery parked in front of a Walmart Supercenter in Hammond, Indiana, about 30 miles to the west.

Rivian (RIVN) stock was up more than 3% this afternoon as the photo made the rounds, according to screenshots shared in the thread. That’s two days before Rivian reports its Q3 2026 results on Thursday, October 29.

Walmart has been trying to electrify last-mile delivery for years. Its supplier picks haven’t aged well.

In 2022, it signed up to buy 4,500 Canoo vans and put them to work on InHome deliveries. Canoo filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in January 2025 and ceased operations.

The same year, Walmart reserved 5,000 BrightDrop vans from GM, and officially added them to its delivery fleet in late 2024. Then GM killed BrightDrop production at its CAMI plant in Ontario a year ago, with no plan to build the van anywhere else. BrightDrop was on pace for roughly 4,000 US sales in 2025, compared to more than 60,000 for GM’s gas-powered Express and Savana vans.

So Walmart is running two orphaned EV van platforms. And if it wants more purpose-built electric vans at scale, the list of US options is very short.

Amazon ordered 100,000 vans from Rivian, and its fleet has now passed 40,000 units on the road. But the deal came with an exclusivity period that ended in November 2023, and Rivian has struggled to land anything close to Amazon-scale since.

AT&T signed up for a pilot in late 2023, and HelloFresh came on board in 2025. In February 2025, Rivian opened van sales to any business, with the RCV 500 starting at $79,900 and the larger RCV 700 at $83,900. None of those customers moves the needle like Walmart would.

There’s also a charging angle. Walmart now operates its own 400 kW fast-charging network at 100 stores in 20 states, and its manager of retail charging, Wade Higgins, previously worked at Rivian, according to his bio on the board of Minnesota car-sharing nonprofit HOURCAR.

One van on a trailer isn’t a fleet order. Not yet, anyway. This could be a test unit for a pilot program, like the one AT&T announced in 2023. And since Rivian sells vans to any business now, Walmart could have simply bought a few to try them out.

So Walmart is running two orphaned EV van platforms. And if it wants more purpose-built electric vans at scale, the list of US options is very short.

Walmart also runs Ford E-Transit vans but I can't find recent numbers for how many

But the timing makes sense. Walmart bet on Canoo and GM, and both left it with vans nobody builds anymore. If you’re Walmart and you want to keep electrifying same-day delivery, Rivian is the obvious call. Its plant in Normal, Illinois, has already built tens of thousands of these vans, and the platform has been proven at scale by the one company Walmart is trying to beat on delivery.

That’s the awkward part. Walmart putting its brand on the same van as Amazon Prime is a bit funny, and it says a lot about how thin the electric van market has gotten in the US.

For Rivian, a Walmart deal would matter. The van business gives it volume in Normal while R2 ramps, and it badly needs proof that the van isn’t just an Amazon product. We’ll see if Rivian says anything on Thursday’s call. We wouldn’t bet on a massive order announcement, but a Walmart pilot wouldn’t surprise us one bit.

#4822. BYD’s $10,000 EV blows a tire at nearly 90 mph — Watch what happens

BYD updated its lowest-priced electric car, the Seagull, which starts at around $10,000 in China, with a few extras, including a high-speed tire blowout system that stabilizes the vehicle at nearly 90 mph.

If the $10,000 price tag wasn’t enough, BYD is giving buyers even more reason to check out its entry-level electric hatch.

The Seagull is among BYD’s most popular vehicles, sold as the Dolphin Surf in Europe and the UK and as the Dolphin Mini in other global markets.

BYD launched the second-generation Seagull EV last week, starting at just 62,900 yuan, or about $9,500. That’s including BYD’s limited-time Super Trade-In incentive.

Regular prices start at 65,900 yuan ($9,900), which is still less than its predecessor. The first-generation Seagull EV started at 69,900 yuan ($10,500) without incentives, making it BYD’s most affordable purely electric vehicle in China.

For its second generation, the Seagull is bigger, more advanced, and adds a bit more luxury to the entry-level segment.

The new BYD Seagull is 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and has a 150 mm longer wheelbase than the previous model.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s electric hatch now offers room for five passengers, up from four seats that the first-gen Seagull had.

BYD added several new features with its latest tech, including a bigger 15.6″ infotainment screen with its DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a “140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system” as standard.

To showcase how the tire blowout system works, BYD put the updated electric hatch to the test at full speed.

BYD’s general manager of the Ocean Series, Zhang Zhuo, shared a video of the second-generation Seagull EV handling the blowout at 140 km/h, or about 87 mph, like it’s nothing.

The high-speed tire-blowout system lets the Seagull stay in its lane until it comes to a complete stop. Pretty impressive for an entry-level vehicle.

As you can see in the video, the new version also has an available roof-mounted LiDAR. Buyers can upgrade to the optional DiPilot 300 system with BYD’s God’s Eye intelligent driving assistance. The ADAS system provides features like City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

BYD added a few premium extras, including heating, ventilation, and a massage function to the front seats, plus ambient lighting, smart storage options, and a 50W wireless phone charger.

The new Seagull uses BYD’s Blade Batteries 2.0 and Flash Charging Technology. As such, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. A full recharge, or 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes 12 minutes to charge from 20% to 97%.

It’s available with two LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh, providing CLTC ranges of 320 km (199 miles) and 420 km (261 miles), respectively.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

The USA is now like a third world country when it comes to Electric Cars.

BYD is leaving the US so far behind in technology, it obviously it will never catch up as a result of it’s backwards MAGA leadership.

The second-gen Seagull also switches to front-wheel-drive (FWD) with a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) that its predecessor offered.

BYD’s new Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000), without a trade-in.

After launching the second-gen Seagull in China, BYD is expected to introduce the updated version overseas. It will likely be the second-generation Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.
